Musical virtuoso and the undisputed GOAT of song parodies 'Weird Al' Yankovic has confirmed his inclusion in GTA 6 as a radio host.

Earlier this week, Weird Al posted saying, "Apologies in advance to any friends or loved ones who may want to have some kind of human interaction with me in the upcoming week. I'll be playing a video game." While that seemed very much in line with the litany of people – famous or otherwise – who are going to dedicate their time to GTA 6 over the next week or so, as people got access to the game , they realized it's weirder than they thought. Vice City FM – home of '80s bangers like Prefab Sprout's Cars and Girls and The The's This Is the Day – is hosted by Mr Yankovic himself.

In a post on BlueSky, Weird Al posts an image saying, "now that my NDA has expired… Hey, everybody, I'm in GTA 6." He adds, "I'm the host of GTA 6's 'non-stop '80s' radio channel Vice City FM," which most people had already gathered, marking his second-ever video game appearance after being the announcer for The Grim Adventures of Billy and Mandy – a Power Stone clone for the PS2 and Wii.

I’m the host of GTA 6’s “non-stop ‘80s” radio channel Vice City FM. I also wrote some in-game commercials, and I’m the voice of the Burger Shot ads as well! As a long-time fan of the Grand Theft Auto franchise, I couldn’t be more excited about this. Okay, gotta get back to playing the game!

But as it turns out, his contributions are more than just a radio host. Weird Al confirms "I also wrote some in-game commercials, and I'm the voice of the Burger Shot ads as well!" The game's credits also list him as a contributor of original music for the game – although unfortunately none of his songs are featured on the in-game radio stations. He adds, "As a long-time fan of the Grand Theft Auto franchise, I couldn't be more excited about this. Okay, gotta get back to playing the game!"

Weird Al is joined by the likes of pop icons Robyn, Gloria Estefan, and PinkPantheress, as well as Fleetwood Mac's Lindsey Buckingham, Yacht Rock king Michael McDonald and Oscar, Tony, Emmy, and Golden Globe winning actor Jeremy Irons as DJ Dicky.

#3801. "Abducting your own lover no longer gives you opinion of yourself" declare the notes for Crusader Kings 3's free Florin update, released alongside Silk and Silver

Funky feudal family frolic Crusader Kings 3 got its second major expansion of the year this week. It's called Silk and Silver (read my impressions), is all about merchant republics, and shipped alongside a beefy free update to the base game which - while largely focused on overhauling economics - also has some funny patch notes and features worth being aware of.

The main features of the free 'Florin' update are outlined by Paradox in the video above, and unless you're really into the nitty gritty details of realm and wealth management, there's one bit of it which stands out. The option to play as a landless adventurer has finally made its way into the base game, as Paradox promised earlier this year.

This means you can kick off a playthrough as a lowborn leader of a travelling band or a wandering noble with claims on realms ruled by others. Originally locked behind the Roads to Power DLC, the option to start off this way or end up living if you end up deposed from your throne of choice is a great addition to the story arc of any CK3 run. No longer are you glued to the throne from day one to the day you quit for good - power's a privilege which can be earned and revoked depending on what you get up to. Though, it's worth noting that only three ways of operating as a landless adventurer are being made free to access with this update. You can be an aimless wanderers, sword-toting mercenaries, or scholars. If you want your band to earn their living as explorers, free booters, or legitimists, you'll still need Roads to Power.

#3800. Infinity Nikki Players Are Planning To ‘Girl-cott’ The Game Over Maye Musk Ad

Infold Games, developers of Love and Deepspace and Infinity Nikki, are 0 for 2 in pissing off their international fanbase for both games. Earlier this year, the studio announced, then cancelled, Love and Deepspace‘s sixth love interest, the werewolf Valko, inspiring some players to go on a sustained boycott that seems to have had a noticeable impact on the gacha game’s revenue in the months since. Now some Infinity Nikki players are hoping to achieve a similar effect, planning a “girl-cott” after Chinese ads for the dress-up gacha game featured Maye Musk, mom of noted racist and transphobe Elon Musk.

Beyond the practical discussions of how exactly to inform Infold Games of player dissatisfaction, girl-cott conversations on the Infinity Nikki subreddit have devolved into thorny back-and-forths on where to draw the line about the thing you enjoy. Some players can’t play the game in good conscience, knowing that Infold Games would choose to partner with the mother of guy who said he fed the USAID organization, responsible for providing food and medical assistance to countries in need, “into the woodchipper,” an act projected to result in widespread death, infection, and suffering for millions, including children. Others don’t see the issue because Maye Musk is not her son, however odious he may be, and the antipathy for him seems to be a uniquely American sentiment with little bearing in the wider, international (and Chinese) Infinity Nikki community.

As a player of both Infinity Nikki and Love and Deepspace, it’s interesting to see both communities arrive at the same fracture point in their relationships with their respective games over two very different events. It’s too early to tell how much of an impact the girl-cott will have, but its timing will no doubt hamper the momentum of the game’s upcoming 3.0 release later this month. If this girl-cott is anything like what happened with Love and Deepspace, Infold Games is once again looking at potential losses in the millions.

#3798. Call of Duty might have swapped guns and tanks for knights and swords if an Infinity Ward experiment had panned out

"If it's a war story, sure, it can be COD."

As much as Call of Duty is criticised for delivering the same thing every year, reports occasionally surface of attempts to take the series in bold new directions, even if none of these experiments have so far seen the light of day. And it turns out a medieval Call of Duty was also explored at one time.

This latest revelation comes from Infinity Ward veteran Taylor Kurosaki, who led development on the studio's Infinite Warfare and 2019 Modern Warfare game. "Call of Duty is a massive tree with a lot of branches, right?" Kurosaki told PC Gamer. "It can be World War 2. The team at IW had prototyped a medieval Call of Duty. Where you were a knight and had a sword and all kinds of crazy shit. But if it's a war story, sure, it can be Call of Duty."

This isn't the first time we've heard of an unusual Call of Duty prototype. When Activision brought Sledgehammer Games into the fold as another lead studio for the lucrative shooter series, the team briefly worked on a third-person horror off-shoot set in Vietnam, which was referred to as Fog of War.

Activision's legal battle with Infinity Ward founders Vince Zampella and Jason West, however, caused the project to be cancelled, as Sledgehammer was roped into helping the studio finish Modern Warfare 3.

As for Kurosaki, he currently leads That's No Moon alongside creative partner Jacob Minkoff and other Infinity Ward and Naughty Dog veterans. The studio is currently working on Crossfire, a narrative-driven third-person shooter set in the universe of Smilegate's free-to-play series of the same name.

#3797. Korridor turns those Youtube ads for vertical mobile shooters into a new, "deeply strategic" genre, and I can't decide if it's lying

The electro-metal OST seems legit, at least

I like to think I'm difficult to hypnotise, but I confess, I'm a sucker for those Youtube adverts for the mobile vertical shooters. You know the ones: boglins pour towards an auto-firing player, who must dodge about to grab upgrades while whittling down the horde. The player in the advert always does pretty well for 20 seconds, but ahhhh, then they get just a tiny bit overconfident, mistime how long it'll take them to erode the health of an ogre midboss, and: bam!

Show me one of those ads, and I'll always watch to the end in the hope that this time, the protagonist will Study The Blade, conquer their harmatia, and slay the damn ogre. I've never actually played any of the mobile shooters in question, mind you. I'm far too cultured for that, you dope! Except that I've just been playing the demo for Korridor, which is supposedly "based off" of the ads, but might as well be one of the games they're promoting, for all I know.

Per the Steam page, it claims to have turned the above advert format into a whole new "deeply strategic genre", the "gates shooter", by stirring in "elements of roguelikes and bullet heavens". I need somebody to authenticate whether this is a truthful statement, or developer TinyToad pulling a fast one. In the meantime, I'll say that 1) I have now managed to kill several ogres, 2) I like Korridor's electro-metal soundtrack.

In Korridor, you're a bald medieval monk garbed in Poundshop Adeptus Astartes platemail. You've woken up in a dungeon of mysterious provenance, and must walk very slowly down its corridors korridors while shooting and punching goblins, wraiths and demons hurrying the other way. Each enemy has a numerical health indicator, and the basic challenge is working out whether you can empty it before they walk into you – which costs you a proportionate amount of health, mitigated by armour. As you go, you'll walk through a choice of gates that grant buffs such as faster health regen, bullet penetration, or nippier horizontal motion.

The fact that you don't control how fast the monk trudges vertically allows the game to synch the onslaught pretty tightly to the thudding, growling score. It reminds me a little of Thumper, though it isn't nearly so invigoratingly malevolent. So far. At intervals, the beat thickens and all the enemies burst into a sprint, throwing their arms up and conveying the strong impression that they are more running away from something than running at you. There's clearly a dreadful entity at the far end of the dungeon. Perhaps it is another overdressed monk with an even bigger gun.

Is this how those mobile games actually work? If it is, then alas and alack, all is lost. I've finally succumbed to those adverts, and all it took was some disingenuous Steam copy promising to place them at a critical remove. Curse you, TinyToad. Curse you and your gates. If you were actually a toad, I'd step on you. Still, now that we've broken the ice, can you please make another game in which I get to play one of those gloating giantesses in Hero Wars? Because I know some people who dig that kind of thing.

#3795. World of Warcraft: Forever isn't mere nostalgia bait - it's rebuilding the MMO social architecture that Blizzard spent years dismantling

And when I fall in love, will it be (WoW) Forever?

I don't play video games regularly anymore. Not because I've lost interest in them, but because I no longer make the time, the premium on which has seemed to exponentiate with age. I realised, however, in 2019 that I was a kind of sleeper agent: whenever I heard the opening notes of Legends of Azeroth, the original World of Warcraft login screen music, I would feel the reactivation of a latent part of my mind laid down when I was 10 years old. And so, like a form of possession, whenever Blizzard announces a new legacy iteration of the original WoW, no downpayment in time nor money is too great to prevent me from returning.

Here I am, then, at the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever, seven years after Blizzard first revived the original 2004 game with World of Warcraft Classic in 2019. Once more I set foot on Durotar, to spend as much time as I can levelling up a new Orc Warrior before I am forcibly unplugged by either my boss or, more likely, my wife, and so far it's been a welcome return to some of the frictional - but more involving and consequential - socialising that WoW's decades of updates had previously sanded down.

My relationship with Azeroth began in 2007, when I was ten years old. As soon as I inserted the CD-ROM, I knew that I was going to have to vastly increase my timeshare on the family desktop. For the next six years, school attendance, sleep, and quality family time suffered immensely as I battled to balance my new parallel existence as a member of the Orcish Horde.

It's unremarkable now, but the fact that characters created at WoW's launch are now 22 years old and can still be played in the latest iteration of the game would have been almost inconceivable to many developers at the turn of the century. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the video game industry was overwhelmingly organised around discrete releases expected to have relatively short lives. For most games, commercial success was concentrated in a brief period surrounding their launch, after which sales declined and eventually ceased. WoW's extraordinary success, and exceedingly long half-life, demonstrated the commercial possibilities and durability of a different model: an evolving, immersive digital environment that players paid to inhabit, year after year. Rather than simply purchasing a finished product, players entered a world that would continue to grow around them. New players, after buying the game (and then its subsequent expansions) and paying for a subscription, could begin their adventures in the same world as those who had been there from the beginning, making their way through its ever-expanding geography and history.

The persistence of Azeroth has been the main driver of its abiding allure for me. I have returned to the game time after time, often just to be enveloped in an audiovisual environment that I know so intimately, and which was so formative in my life. But as the WoW universe was continually developed, the game became increasingly unrecognisable from the version I skipped school to play on Windows XP.

What I wanted from the game had also changed. In a turn that would have been completely anathema to my teenage self, I no longer cared about reaching the endgame or having the most competitive character. I stopped caring about the latest raiding content or PvP rankings. Instead, the elements of the game I had once feverishly tried to skip over, like levelling, professions and story, became, ironically, the only parts of the game that I yearned for.

As time unspooled, WoW naturally needed updates to stay fresh. This meant overhauling many of the unwieldy elements of its original design. Much of this was described as 'streamlining' the player experience, making the game less tedious by reducing downtime and, most critically, reliance on other players.

The original Azeroth emulated the real world in ways that few contemporary games do. Firstly, it was openly unbalanced, with some classes vastly stronger than others, some of which were borderline unplayable. Secondly, it required extraordinary amounts of patience and downtime to navigate. Most importantly, though, it required collaboration with others to get the most out of it. In order to access the latest content, players would have to self-organise into specifically composed groups as big as 40 players large, and schedule lengthy chunks of time each week to make progress.

Over time, much of the original social architecture that forced player collaboration was stripped from the game. Adventurers no longer needed to search for and group up with other players from their own server to complete rewarding content. Automated matchmaking systems increasingly did the work for them.

I remember many late nights when I was prevented from doing something quite modest because there were simply not enough players online, or not enough of the right classes. With my ambitions frustrated, I would often have no choice but to log off and try again in the morning. These frustrations were, I only learnt in retrospect, an important byproduct of inhabiting a world that did not exist solely for my benefit. Other people had their own schedules, priorities and ambitions, and my experience of the game depended on those contingencies.

The changes to WoW followed the trajectory of the wider online gaming industry, where players could increasingly be matched instantly with others at any time of day. These were changes that genuinely respected players' time, but the texture and immersion of the game world paid a hefty price. In making the game more convenient, Blizzard had also made it less necessary, and in some respects less possible, to participate in the social world that had once made Azeroth feel so alive.

It became increasingly clear that there was a subset of players, like me, who weren't interested in seeing an old dog learn new tricks, and just wanted to spend time with the old girl we'd raised from a pup. Even if she did walk slowly, and was a bit blind.

As the years went on, many players moved on with their lives, even if they continued to carry some indelible residue of Azeroth with them. Others created unofficial instances of the original game, known as private servers, and relived those infant years with a knowledge of the world that they could scarcely have imagined possessing when they first entered it. As these servers became increasingly popular, Blizzard, originally very reluctant, eventually launched Classic in 2019, an official revival of the game in something approaching its original 2004 form. Since then, legacy versions of WoW have become popular enough to exist alongside the modern game as a major branch of the franchise.

Re-releasing these legacy versions has been a considerable commercial success. But it also exposed a problem with the project of preservation. The original game, because it is so timeworn, has effectively been 'solved.' Players know almost everything about it, including its most obscure idiosyncrasies, and have found ingenious ways of exploiting them. The uncertainty that once made Azeroth feel so vast and mysterious has been replaced by an extraordinary collective expertise. When new content was added to the game, even the best guilds would spend weeks making no progress. During those early years, players at Azeroth's frontiers had to innovate to find creative ways of tackling novel and seemingly intractable problems.

There are clear limits to simulating a turning back of the clock. Players like me slowly realised that we didn't simply want to return to an earlier, simpler period in Azeroth. We wanted something impossible. Like the characters in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, we wanted to forget what we already knew so that we might experience our birth in Azeroth for the first time all over again.

WoW: Forever is an attempt to solve this problem. Like Old School RuneScape, Forever's undeniable forerunner and a considerable success in its own right, it is an expanded re-release of the original game that imagines an alternate future for Azeroth: one in which the game continues to evolve without abandoning the original texture and mechanics, and one that preserves the social architecture that made it so enriching in the first place.

As I write this, my Orc Warrior is sitting at a Campfire, a new mechanic that allows players to establish communal campsites and contribute profession-specific items that confer temporary bonuses to themselves and others. To receive a benefit from Campfires, adventurers are forced to sit together, a deliberate attempt from Blizzard to encourage interactions between players. It is too early to tell how effective this socialising mechanism will be in the long run, but nearly everyone in my experience so far has been eager to shoot the breeze together. I have already shared a number of conversations with other players, most of whom are thirty- or forty-somethings on a similar nostalgia quest as me.

I am playing the game on a laptop using a trackpad, caring very little about efficient or optimal progression. Although I suspect a substantial proportion of the player base shares my approach, not everyone has approached the game so casually. At least five players have already reached maximum level, and many others will have meticulously theory-crafted plans designed to skip straight to the endgame. This is a good thing, and the game should be able to support players with different goals. It's important that the game rewards time and effort, but I hope that the modest amount of time I am able to commit will allow me to feel like I am on my own meaningful adventure, and not a weak player who is trailing behind.

Many in the community have come to believe, perhaps wishfully, that Forever might escape the trap of vertical progression, in which each new wave of content supersedes and renders older content redundant. Instead, the promise of horizontal progression, where new content expands the range of meaningful activities and rewards available without continually raising the ceiling of character power, has been latched on to by members of the community, even though Blizzard's messaging in this regard has not been totally clear.

For players like me, the appeal of horizontal progression is that Azeroth might once again become a place to inhabit, rather than a race to finish. I want to be able to wander off, pursue some obscure profession, or spend an evening doing very little of consequence without feeling that the rest of the world has left me behind. I know I don't have the time to commit to the endgame hamster wheel, and whether Forever will produce a gameworld that meaningfully accommodates players with such different ambitions remains to be seen. But for now, at least, it feels good to be home.

#3794. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 is the US' best-selling physical game so far this year

The very popular and critically-acclaimed The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has set another record. After selling 5.2m copies in four days and becoming the Switch 2's fastest-selling game, Ocarina of Time has now been revealed to also be a major seller at retail.

The remake has sold more than 1m physical copies in the US alone in its launch week (ending 7th November). That's according to Circana analyst Mat Piscatella, who revealed on Bluesky that the record also makes it the first title to surpass 1m physical sales since 2023's Tears of the Kingdom. That is, no other game - from any publisher - has managed to sell over 1m copies in the US within its first week in three years.

While Nintendo games tend to perform better at retail than those from Sony, Xbox or third-party publishers, physical sales in general have been declining in the US. In July, Piscatella revealed that just seven PlayStation games have sold more than 100,000 physical copies up to that point in 2026, and that was after all the backlash to Sony's decision to end physical disc manufacturing by January 2028.

Ocarina of Time's lead of this particular segment likely won't continue, however. That's because, as Piscatella pointed out in a follow-up post, Circana's tracking considers disc-less, code-in-box versions to be physical editions. This means Grand Theft Auto 6 will likely overtake the remake in short order, just as it's expected to break records elsewhere.

In Eurogamer's glowing review of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, Christian Donlan argued that Nintendo has done just enough to modernise a timeless classic while maintaining what made the original so special for many players.

EXCLUSIVE: This is Lenovo's upcoming Legion Go Beam, a new gaming handheld that appears to be a more affordable alternative to the premium Legion Go 2: https://t.co/T5Nrh5VAig pic.twitter.com/JdLI9QrzsKNovember 18, 2026

With the pricing of memory right now, it's hard to get too excited for gaming handhelds, but Lenovo's reportedly more budget-friendly Legion Go Beam does intrigue me. And, with a recent leak, I'm now looking forward to hearing about the full details in the new year.

This leak comes courtesy of Windows Latest, which managed to get its hands on three images, plus the name, and a suggestion that it will be less expensive than the Legion Go 2. Admittedly, the Legion Go 2 and its OLED screen are climbing up to $2,000 right now, so undercutting that isn't super tough.

The Go Beam has a white shell with lime green accents at the bottom, on the face buttons, around the thumbsticks, and on the start and menu buttons. It's a striking theme, even if I fear grubby fingers will make that white far grimmer in a matter of months.

There is, unfortunately, a lot we don't know about this handheld. We don't know the screen's panel technology; we don't know what size and weight it is; we don't know what processor powers it; we don't have a price point, and we don't yet have a release date.

Windows Latest is guessing it will be cheaper than the Legion Go based on its feature set, which is not a bad call.

You get most of the controls you expect from a modern handheld, with triggers and bumpers, as well as two paddles on the back. There's a single USB Type-C port on the top of the device, and it has a sequence of eight fan holes in the back left.

It is, however, missing the small touchpad under the right thumbstick that comes with the Lenovo Legion Go S (both Windows and SteamOS models). That means navigating the desktop UI could be a little less easy, though at launch it wasn't usable in SteamOS anyways. It also has bigger bezels than the Go 2 and Go S.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

Lenovo has been very fond of AMD with its gaming handhelds thus far, using Ryzen Z2, Z2 Extreme and Ryzen Z2 Go chips, but there is a suggestion the Beam could be kitted with a lower-end Panther Lake chip (perhaps the Intel Arc G3 and its Arc B370 iGPU). I haven't spent much time with the G3, but I have been very impressed with the G3 Extreme, from both a performance and battery life perspective.

With Lenovo attending CES at the start of 2027, Windows Latest reckons that is when we will see more about this handheld. But it does note that Lenovo doesn't mention gaming for the January show, so it could be holding out for later in 2027, perhaps Computex in June.

Either way, if Lenovo is putting out cheaper handhelds, that's certainly not bad news for us PC gamers, even if we're still going to be paying an arm and a leg for the memory and storage inside it.

#3791. Rockstar firings tribunal hears closing statements, with judge promising to deliver a verdict "as quickly as I possibly can" - though it may take a while

The employment tribunal over Rockstar's firing of 34 workers last year has come to an end for now, pending a final verdict from the judge. Said judge hasn't offered a concrete estimate of when her judgement will arrive, but has reportedly asserted that she'll provide it "as quickly as [she] possibly can".

That's according to People Make Games' Chris Bratt, who's reported on the tribunal throughout the proceedings."I cannot give a time frame for producing the judgement in this case," he cited judge Lucy Wiseman as having said following closing arguments from Rockstar and the union representing the fired staff over the past couple of days. "What I will say is that I will use my best [endeavours] to get that judgement out as quickly as I possibly can."

Bratt reported that could mean anything from weeks to a few months of waiting, leaving the fired staff looking at more time in the limbo they've occupied throughout the tribunal.

To recap the arguments Wiseman will have heard, Rockstar accused the fired staff of leaking "confidential information on a public forum", while the Independent Workers’ union of Great Britain (IWGB) union have accused Rockstar of being motivated by union busting in letting the workers go. According to a previous report from People Make Games, discussion of a new company Slack policy in a union-run Discord server preceded the firings.

The fired devs haven't called for supporters to boycott GTA 6 - the game they were working on prior to being let go - in solidarity, but instead to consider buying specially-designed union t-shirts, the proceeds of which will go towards the workers' "Fighting Fund".

Devs still at Rockstar and the IWGB have formed the Rockstar Games Workers Union since their fired colleagues' tribunal proceedings began and are in the midst of a vote on union recognition as of writing.

Writing in The Guardian's Comment Is Free section this week, Rockstar animation programmer Nestor Uriarte expressed that it's "hard not to worry about what the future holds" for developers at the studio, with the prospect of layoffs potentially happening now the big game is out the door concerning staff. Uriarte made clear that, as of the writing of his piece, Rockstar staff "have had no indication that layoffs are coming".

#3790. Maingear's revamped Zero range is already selling out, and I can see why

The revamped version of the Maingear Zero feels even more bespoke to its cable-less design philosophy. With a homemade case and cooler from Maingear itself, the Mk.2 doubles down on what made this PC great to begin with. It's a gaming desktop that emphasises this brand's pristine build quality, and one that will be an absolute showstopper to have in your setup. It comes at a premium though, and not just because of the RAMpocalypse.

Harder to upgrade if you aren't well-versed in back-connect motherboards

Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy.

2026 is a dreadful time to be shopping for a new desktop PC. I know that; you probably all know that, and PC hardware brands who are struggling to shift any new products due to massive price inflations definitely know that. For many, the current economy means upgrading is written off entirely, because the expense is just too high at the moment. But when the going gets tough, the tough get going, and Maingear's latest attempt to reinstate itself as the best gaming PC builder embodies that.

It seems to me that Maingear understands the following; if gamers are going to upgrade their PC at the moment, it might as well be for a good reason. In other words, the products on offer need to be flawless to entice people to buy them because they really need to be worth the added expense they bring. When I reviewed the first rendition of the Maingear Zero Ruby back in 2024, I already thought it was worth its premium price tag, not just because the computer itself was beautiful, but because this brand makes a point of going the extra mile with its products on behalf of its customers.

Back then, the Zero's concept was novel - it was the first range of prebuilt PCs to use back-connect motherboards. But at some point in 2025, the Zero range quietly disappeared from Maingear's store, only seeing a revival this year alongside the revamped MG-1 flagship the brand prides itself on. This Mk.2 rendition of the Zero is going to cost you more than the original ever did, but it makes modern enhancements that would tempt any PC gamer into ignoring the RAMpocalypse and slapping their money down on the table.

I mean, just look at this thing. The panoramic glass, the multi-angle AIO cooler display, the seven pre-installed fans, the absolutely spotless build quality? It takes the novel idea of a PC with zero visible cables we saw two years ago and takes it to the next level.

Case in point, this PC was actually really difficult to take review photos of because its fancy, futuristic glass meant no matter the angle I snapped from, I'd be somewhere in the reflection. That's an annoyance for me, but a very, very good thing for you because this is the sort of PC that displays your components beautifully, and something you'll want on display as the heart of your gaming setup. Don't put this thing under your desk - it's something to show off.

I went to Computex this year; I've seen some innovations in fans, I've seen new case designs that look fancy and futuristic, and I've seen mice with upward-firing fans in them. But I think the Zero Mk.2 might be the best-looking bit of gaming PC hardware I've seen this year. The adoption of panoramic glass is huge, but the way it works in tandem with a cooler that's visible from every angle takes the clean, cableless design philosophy to new heights. It also manages to look bigger on the inside than it actually is, but more on that in a minute.

First, we have to talk about the build quality - which I shouldn't be surprised by, knowing Maingear as a brand, but I still was. There are often nitpicks I have with prebuilt gaming PCs when I review them. For example, the GPU bracket Quoted Tech chose in the PC they sent was blatantly wrong, causing friction with an intake fan and making an annoying whirring sound. Especially having built and rebuilt my own PCs for years now, these things can be easy to spot. But I went through the Maingear Zero Mk.2 with a fine-toothed comb; there's nothing to pick apart. In the box, there's even a checklist to evidence the PC you've received has been built to high standards and stress-tested before it even gets to you. This time around, I even saw improvements on the first Zero.

Hardware nerds unite, sign up to our free tech newsletter for a weekly digest of the hottest new tech, the latest gadgets on the test bench, and much more from the team at GamesRadar+.

The annoying GPU support bracket from the original was so integrated into the motherboard that even to add a new SSD in, you had to disassemble the entire graphics card and faceplate first. This has been improved so it's more practical this time around.

Something else that I love is that Maingear has opted for a pretty reasonably sized chassis for the revamped Zero. As far as I'm aware, it's Maingear's own, homemade Zero Mk.2 case, which wasn't the case last time, as MSI's MAG Pano M100 PZ was borrowed for it - presumably as part of whatever deal was struck to get hold of the brand's motherboards.

This time around, Maingear has taken a lot of design notes from Cooler Master, MSI, Asus, and now NZXT with their curved-glass PC cases. But the actual physical size of this chassis is a compact mATX that fits ATX boards. It means the PC can be a reasonable size that'll fit on top of your desk, in a showy position in your room, or in a tighter space in a smaller gaming room.

When the first batch of Zero PCs hit the shelves, these motherboards were still relatively new on the scene; they were quirky and were harder to come by. Now, their concept isn't so novel, and there's a larger range of boards, including smaller mATX ones that help Maingear to keep things compact here.

Of course, one downside in grabbing a PC like this with a back-connect motherboard is that maintaining that pristine look over the years might make things difficult. If you want to upgrade one of these rigs but you're not that sure of how to perform various PC surgeries, the advice you find online will only be harder to follow if you take on a motherboard that isn't conventional. Furthermore, it's going to be very difficult not to disrupt Maingear's very neat and tidy PC assembly job when you upgrade, so it feels like there would be a risk of messing things up if you go to upgrade your machine later. That's just something to think about.

As you can see, the ceiling for the new range of Zero PCs is a bit ludicrous, with the Amethyst configuration (which is the closest comparison to my review unit) costing $7,299 at the time of writing. Yes, you did read that right.

Some interesting disparities between the version I tested and what you'll get are that, while I had a B860 chipset for an AMD processor, you can have either an AMD CPU for gaming or an Intel Core Ultra 200S Plus one - this is one of the few pre-built PCs outside of custom builds that allow you to configure either an AMD or Intel chipset.

Also interesting is that I had XPG RAM, while all the other versions of the Zero Mk.2 are advertised to have Kingston Fury memory in them. I don't imagine the reason I was sent something different was anything to do with hiding the performance you'll get - it's probably much more likely that Maingear was using whatever it had stock of for my temporary review unit.

Alongside this top-of-the-range configuration though, the Zero Mk.2 comes in an "Elite" version harnessing an RTX 5080. Right now, all of the named, prebuilt variations of the new Ruby are sold out, but you can still fully customize one to be built to your exact specifications. From what I gather on Maingear's builder, the Zero starts at $2,988, with minimum component options being an 8GB RTX 5060 Ti, AMD Ryzen 5 9600X, 32GB of RAM, and 2TB SSD.

If you do want to spare yourself some expense, Maingear does have a BYO-RAM option which might help to take that minimum spend down a touch. Funnily enough, I remember criticising the configurations of the original Maingear Zero for so many of them only offering 16GB of DDR5 despite their high prices. Now, during RAMageddon, the minimum this sequel PC comes with is 32GB.

As is always the case when I'm supplied with a review unit that spares absolutely no expense when it comes to power, these performance figures are going to be relevant to you only if you opt for a 5090 configuration. Do not expect these kinds of numbers if you opt for the more affordable 5060 Ti versions of this machine. Still, I'm always going to put a review model through its paces, and I was particularly keen to see if aesthetically flawless building amounted to strong performance.

The GPU being an RTX 5090, I can happily say that no PSU cables spontaneously combusted during this review - I'd love to say this is a solid sign that thermals are being handled well by the new Maingear Zero Mk.2 case, but that may just be luck of the draw with the GPU, PSU, and its cables.

On that note, the GPU was actually warmer during my testing than the CPU, with the Ryzen 7 only peaking at 69 degrees Celsius during 3DMark's Time Spy benchmark, while the RTX 5090 reached 73 degrees. Elsewhere in benchmarking the CPU had higher peaks, but the GPU had higher mean temperatures overall, which tells you a lot about the 5090. At the same time, credit where it's due goes to the Maingear 360mm AIO cooler, which kept the beefy X3D processor cool under strenuous workloads.

Cinebench:Multi Thread: 5605ptsSingle Core: 761ptsSingle Thread: 562pts

3DMark:TimeSpy: 36,896Firestrike: 66,029Steel Nomad: 140.94fps

CrystalDiskMark:Sequential read: 7,387 MB/sSequential write: 6,769 MB/s

AIDA64 Extreme / RAM readings:59,228 MB/s read30-36-36-76 (6,000MT/s)

One thing I'd like to point out is that, just like the original Maingear Zero, something that really stands out about this brand's computers is that they buck the trend of most PC builders by supplying some really top-rate RAM and SSDs. Usually, this is where pre-build companies make a bit of money back because they'll give you the headline GPU and CPU specs you want, but the quality of the RAM and SSDs will be lesser because they don't matter quite so much. Maingear's attitude is a little different, because it wants to give you nothing but the best parts, and it shows in testing.

The SSD here achieved a 7,000+MB/s read speed, which is what you'd hope for when it comes to a Gen 4 NVMe M.2 SSD - a lot of the time PCs can house SSDs that get stuck in the 5,000s, which is okay, but not great for the money you pay for one of these Zero Mk.2 rigs. At a time like this, when SSDs and RAM will be harder to come by and cost you more, that could be a good or a bad thing, but at least you know you're getting quality parts here - perhaps more affordably than if you were to buy separately due to Maingear likely buying in bulk and having partnerships with suppliers like TeamGroup.

I'd love to applaud the fact that the RAM aboard the Zero Mk.2 achieved a higher AIDA Extreme reading than desktops I've tested previously, but since it's not the standard memory from Kingston you'll receive in your machine, it may not matter so much. If you choose to bring your own RAM to the Zero Mk.2, the benchmarks above will at least show you what's possible.

It's no surprise at all that, seeing as this is actually the first 5090 rig I've reviewed so far this generation, the gaming and software benchmarks are the highest you'll see in any chart.

The RTX 5090 is a ridiculous piece of kit, but even before the RAMpocalypse, it was always priced out of reach of the majority of gamers. Even to begin with, I don't think the RTX 5090 was really designed for gamers anyway, and it was mainly designed, as the 4090 was, for AI users, crypto mining, pro-level 3D artists, and content creators. Keep that in mind while looking at the benchmarks here. They're absurdly powerful, but probably not what most gamers will actually need when buying even a premium-level PC, especially when one like this will currently cost you more than a car.

There's a hell of a combination of parts coming together to work in tandem in these results, and like I say, there's no surprise the Zero Mk.2 has recorded the highest results of any PC I've ever benchmarked.

It'd be easy for me to draw the line there and say, since it's the most powerful PC, it's the best overall, but that'd actually be cutting the Maingear Zero Mk.2 short.

There's more to actually using this PC than its parts that I think makes it the best, and after all, you might not have one with an RTX 5090 in it.

For example, thermals are really solid here, which can sometimes suffer in cases designed specifically to look good. Even under these stressful benchmarks, I don't think I really noticed the fans kicking up much of an audible fuss from under my desk once. The Zero Mk.2 is compact, it's quiet, and it's the most powerful and best-built PC I've come across. Again, the RTX 5090 configuration outguns even some of the other highest-end PCs I've benchmarked, but even with a 5080, I think the stronger supporting components here would mean the Zero Mk.2 could stand a chance at pulling ahead of the competition on performance.

Moreover, while you pay a premium for Maingear goods, you do get some of the best warranty, servicing, and customer service options I've seen from a PC building brand. Maingear PCs get lifetime service and repairs. Even if you pass the PC on to a friend or sell it on, the label and number on the back sticker of the PC means you can quote it to a service agent, and they'll be happy to help with whatever is wrong with the rig.

And the PC that arrives with you has absolutely minimal bloatware other than what Windows insists you have. The sample I received was packaged well with an inner and outer box, expanding foam in case you need to send it back or pack it up during a house move; there are set-up instructions, and everything in the PC comes properly installed so that you don't need to do a thing to get going besides plug things in and get started.

Are this company's PC's constantly in high demand, and do they cost a premium? Yes, and that might be your biggest barrier to entry.

The Maingear Zero Mk.2 has doubled down on what made the original my favorite gaming PC I've tested. It's somehow got an even cleaner build this time around, and its case and cooler only complement that, with a design that lets the cableless beauty within speak for itself.

Maingear has managed to design and execute something that lets you have the best of every world when it comes to buying a new PC. There's a compact size here that makes it versatile for your setup and the way you want to use it. There's an option to cram it with some of the beefiest and best components out there, and it's all something that looks a million dollars without making itself heard due to poor thermals.

That said, I do think this brand should be treated like the holy grail of the prebuilt market. The prices here are high, and yes, you're paying more than you would from other companies for an additional level of quality. But I wouldn't be doing my job if I didn't say there are other PC makers out there that won't charge quite as much and still give you the specs, an attractive design, and great thermals.

I think the people who should be looking for a Maingear Zero Mk.2 are the ones who want an absolute showstopper of a PC that can do it all. For those prepared to spare no expense, there's no PC I'd recommend harder.

I put the Maingear Zero Mk.2 through its paces by using it for around 2 weeks. In that time, I put it through all of the formal benchmarking tests we here at GamesRadar+ use to recommend you new computing tech. I played games with it, I created some video content, and I put it through strict benchmarking tests in both the gaming and content creation software worlds. I kept track of data on frame rates, temperatures, and more.

I also evaluated pricing, tech specs, and Maingear as a brand to come to a verdict.

#3789. Sci-fi RPG Exodus continues evoking Mass Effect by revealing female lead and nicknaming her FemJun

Sci-fi role-playing game Exodus continues to play into the Mass Effect comparisons by revealing the female version of its main character Jun, and with studio Archetype referring to her in marketing material as FemJun.

If that moniker sounds familiar it's because it is: the female Commander Shepard character in the Mass Effect series was nicknamed FemShep. FemShep became an iconic part of BioWare's iconic series, eventually proving that female leads could front games just as successfully as male leads could, and be every bit as popular.

Is the nickname FemJun too blatant? Possibly. But there's well publicised BioWare pedigree at Archetype Entertainment, in the studio's co-founders and in the people leading the project. Key Mass Effect writer Drew Karpyshyn is in charge of writing Exodus, for example, and the similarities to Mass Effect are something the Exodus team has not been shy about in the past. In the wake of Mass Effect 5 being cancelled and BioWare being closed, they become even more alluring.

There are, however, big and important differences between Exodus and Mass Effect, key among them, time dilation. In Exodus, there are special Exodus missions whereby you leave your home planet and fly far away, and in doing so experience time differently to the people back home. Many years will pass for them while only days will pass for you, which provides the game with a way to show you long-term consequences of your actions when you return.

Archetype hasn't shown the female version of Jun before, despite having released many videos of Exodus, perhaps to build anticipation for her reveal. It's a press beat that's also provided Archetype - a studio owned by Dungeons & Dragons company Wizards of the Coast - with an occasion to reveal the two actors playing Jun in the game.

Female Jun is portrayed by Carina Conti, who played the lead in the recent Mafia game, The Old Country - Isabella Torrisi. She's appeared in HBO's Winning Time and Hulu/Freeform's Good Trouble as well. Male Jun, meanwhile, is portrayed by Stephen Oyoung, who played Mister Negative in Insomniac's Marvel's Spider-Man 1 and 2 games, and Red Hood in Gotham Knights. He also appeared in Mission: Impossible - The Final Reckoning, The Wrecking Crew, and Twisters. The game also famously stars Matthew McConaughey.

Archetype announced a Dark Horse hardback art book to go on sale alongside the game next year as well. This arrives a week after the game; Exodus arrives 7th April 2027 on PC, PS5 and Xbox Series S/X, and the art book on 13th April.

Matt played Exodus at Gamescom relatively recently and came away impressed, referring to it as "the best kind of surprise". "I wasn't expecting quite such a bombastic 45 minutes when I first picked up a controller and settled into Exodus, admittedly, but the more I played, the more it made sense," he wrote. "I might not be much of a Mass Effect fan (damn you M35 Mako once more), but Exodus is now firmly on my radar ahead of its arrival next year."

#3788. Hour-long Total War: Warhammer 40,000 campaign stream shows off ship battle-less fleet management, makes clear how not ideal getting Space Marine armies killed is

"It would take them decades to recover from that"

Try not to get whole armies of Space Marines pasted against the surfaces of planets thanks to your shoddy tactics, please. So ask the bosses of Total War: Warhammer 40,000, who're keen not to have their training workloads doubled because you're a crap general and have gotten a tight-knit force of uber-tough grunts killed unnecessarily, hope as they watch you play. This and other things have been emphasised by a fresh stream showing off over an hour of campaigning in the strategy warhammerer.

The stream showed off "an expansion" of the build that devs Creative Assembly let folks like RPS bossman Julian give a go at Gamescom in the summer, via an Ultramarines campaign in a system called Praevoss. Described as a middle-of-the-road option in terms of system size, Praevoss is home to three conquerable planets and a couple of others that aren't suitable for stompy unit hijinks.

Each star system's a "contained campaign", so you hop from one to the next, with certain aspects of your army or skills you've built up carrying over. "First and foremost, we want to represent the scale of the whole galaxy, which is just not possible on a single Total War map," the devs explained. "You'd never be able to engage with it. Part of the point is to break this up a bit and allow us to have some more interesting and more bespoke narratives going on. So each of these star systems has a premise, has a narrative, has a specific setup, a specific start [point], [and] specific victory objectives that you've got to go and do." Creative assembly have also been able to play around a bit more with difficulty as a result of this setup.

As the stream properly got going, the devs focused on chatting about unit specialisation, fleet movement, fleet actions, fleet transportation and Space Marine fleet buildings. Your fleet takes the form of big ships which can be parked above a continent on a planet and offer support via reinforcements and bombardment. As far as the Space Marines specifically go, they're designed to be a small force that's tough to kill, rather than a massive one that's able to recover more quickly and aims to overwhelm with sheer numbers as part of its gameplan.

"Losing a whole army of Space Marines is pretty devastating," the devs said, as if sensing some blunder I might make far in the future. "That's intentional, as that's a whole Space Marine chapter. Like, losing an army of Space Marines, that's a massive deal for them. It would take them decades to recover from that." At least it looks like I'll not be losing any ships too, since their presence seems limited to providing support to the ground troops, rather than battling each other high above the planets.

As of right now, Total War: Warhammer 40,000 remains without a release date, but can be wishlisted on Steam if you fancy.

A Fallout hidden object game? About cats? Color me interested.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A few hours after this story went live, Bethesda confirmed that A Wasteland Full of Cats is indeed legit. "The game offers a cozy new way to explore the Wasteland, as players set out to rescue Fofiño’s missing fiends, discover familiar locations, meet companions along the way, and use their Pip-Kitty to uncover secrets and solve mysteries, one cat at a time," a spokesperson said."Devcats’ mission to raise awareness of animal adoption and rescue makes this partnership a natural fit for Bethesda. Supporting animal rescue is something our teams and community have cared about for many years, including through our long-standing partnership with Dallas Pets Alive, which began in 2015. That shared commitment, together with Devcats’ unique approach to their games, gave us an opportunity to bring those worlds together in a way that feels both meaningful and distinctly Fallout."While some details about the project have surfaced a little earlier than planned, we’re incredibly excited by what the Devcats team has created and the playfully unexpected way they’ve reimagined the world of Fallout. We look forward to sharing more about A Wasteland Full of Cats soon."

I'm not quite sure what to make of this so I'm going to just put it out there: A new Fallout game might soon be headed our way, and it's a hidden object game.

A Wasteland Full of Cats, as it's known, recently appeared on the Australian Classification Board website (via the Fallout subreddit), and the title pretty much says it all. From the rating:

This game is a hidden object game and the objects you need to find are cats. You play as one of the cats in the Vault. One day there is an accident in the Vault and all of the cats who live there escape out into the Wasteland. It is up to you with the help of some NPCs you meet along the way to find them and return them to the Vault. This game has 14 locations, 33 rooms + a vault of recognizable levels from the Fallout franchise with light puzzle mechanics that uncover some hidden levels that aren’t required to finish the game. There is a final boss fight where the player has to shoot some Rad roaches in order to save the last remaining cats and humans.

The rating says A Wasteland Full of Cats is being made by Devcats, the Brazilian studio behind the Full of Cats game series, and—this is the really interesting part—it's being made "in partnership with Bethesda and the Fallout franchise."

Is this legit? Is the next Fallout release a hidden object game? I don't know, but I do know that the Australian Classification Board generally isn't party to pranks and hoaxes. I also know that a lot of Fallout fans will be rolling their eyes and moaning at the idea of hidden object Fallout, but hear me out: Hidden object games are good, actually.

Sure, you're not going to be prowling through horrific underground labs or gunning down super mutants in a life-or-death struggle for survival. But hidden object games are chill and relaxing, a great way to wind down after a busy day robbing liquor stores and shooting cops with your significant other. They're a simpler kind of fun, which makes them kind of kin to the really early days of videogames, when we were all ready to accept that a blocky blob of pink on the screen was a dragon.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

All of which is to say that even if you have no interest in playing a Fallout hidden object game (although I think you should), it's far from unthinkable that Bethesda would make one—or have someone make one for it, I suppose. (I would also point out that you could say basically the same thing about Fallout Shelter, and it's been chugging happily along for well over a decade now.)

#3785. They're more complicated and more expensive than LCD screens, but your next gaming monitor should still be an OLED

Your next gaming monitor should be an OLED display. There, I've said it. And I know the notion won't please everyone. After all, a large grey proboscidean lumbers into the room whenever OLED technology is mentioned. Put simply, almost any risk of the dreaded burn-in is an immediate deal-breaker for some. I do get that.

Likewise, despite my musings just the other day on how affordable gaming monitors have generally become and the fact you can now snag an OLED panel, specifically, for sub £300 / $300, it's a stretch to say OLED gaming comes cheap. And yet here I am arguing firmly in favour of OLED.

The point is that OLED is fundamentally superior to LCD, the latter being the dominant display tech on the PC for decades and also, as it happens, an unambiguous technological kludge. Understanding why is the relatively easy bit. Where things get extraordinarily, even belligerently, complicated concerns the current OLED gaming monitor market and the baffling array of panel types and monitor models on offer.

We'll get to all that. But let's start with the core appeal of OLED, which comes down to two factors: lighting control and speed. In both regards, OLED technology completely annihilates LCD. The thing about OLED panels and lighting is that each pixel is its own individually controlled light source. Actually, each subpixel is.

That means literally perfect lighting control. There's no leakage, no need for bodges like local dimming. Just the ability to have immediately adjacent pixels doing absolutely opposite things, one fully lit up, the other totally off. The impact of that on contrast is epic. In short, if you want a true HDR experience that combines sizzling bright highlights with properly controlled black levels, only OLED can do that.

The problem with LCD, you see, is that it's a transmissive technology, so light is pushed through the pixels from a big, dumb backlight behind. The liquid crystals in each subpixel are then oriented by an electric charge, controlling the quantity and colour of the light output. In practice, there are oh so many limitations to that approach.

Chief among these problems is that the backlight leaks through in all kinds of unintended ways. And let's be clear, technologies like mini-LED backlights with full-array local dimming don't get anywhere near entirely compensating for LCD's shortcomings. For starters, even a mini-LED backlight with 2,000 zones is very, very low resolution in terms of lighting.

With that kind of zone count, you're looking at a backlight resolution of roughly 55 zones by 35 zones in a 16:9 monitor. Imagine if the actual image resolution was 55 by 35 pixels. Yuck. In the context of a 4K monitor, then, each zone is shared across approximately 4,000 pixels. That's a lot and it translates into visible blooming, weird brightness gradients, dimming zones noticeably popping on and off and all that messy, ugly stuff.

While we're talking liquid crystals twisting in the electrical wind, that's also the reason why LCD is so much slower than OLED. It involves the physical rotation of those rod-shaped crystals to update the image. Like I said, the pixels in an OLED panel are their own light-emitting diode sources, and very rapidly reacting ones at that. So, OLED response times are essentially instantaneous from a human perception perspective.

I will admit, it's still impressive how good modern LCD panels can look, despite their numerous baked-in limitations. But in lots of important ways, OLED is inherently more suited to gaming displays than LCD. The catch is that it, too, is imperfect, ye olde burn-in being the most obvious shortcoming.

The "O" in OLED refers to "organic", as in Organic Light Emitting Diode. The "organic" bit translates into carbon-based molecules that degrade with use. In short, the harder you drive an OLED pixel, the more its ability to output light is worn out. Over time, the whole panel will wear to some degree, degrading maximum light output. But the real fear is differential wear that leads to unevenness across the screen. The classic scenario is static on-screen interface furniture, perhaps the Windows task bar or persistent parts of a game interface like a health bar or minimap. Eventually, those elements will lead to uneven panel wear.

Pretty much all current OLED gaming monitors have various burn-in mitigation technologies, such as pixel shift, refresh cycles, edge dimming and so on. But none entirely solve the problem. As for real-world expectations of just how bad burn-in can be, there are several independent assessments of OLED monitor burn-in. For instance, Monitors Unboxed has been running one that's now at the 30-month mark, testing absolute worst-case usage on the MSI MPG 321URX, which is from the first generation of 4K, Samsung-made QD-OLED panels.

For what it's worth, my overall view - based on both personal experience with numerous OLED panels over the last few years, and what you might call the emerging consensus - is that burn-in is a real problem, but shouldn't stop most of us buying an OLED. The aforementioned worst-case scenario usage includes driving the panel hard in terms of brightness settings, routine use of persistent interface elements and even failing to allow burn-in mitigation measures to run optimally. Basically, doing all the wrong things. And the evidence is that even this doesn't lead to truly catastrophic burn-in.

After a year of really heavy daily use, you'll probably see some very slight burn-in that's only visible if you go out of your way to look for it. In the second and third years, the burn-in will become more apparent, but only gradually, and even then it will likely still only be visible in certain situations, like an application window with a uniform grey background. The panel will also experience a touch of overall brightness drop off, but not enough to be subjectively noticeable.

All of that applies to early OLED monitors released three to four years ago, starting with the Alienware 34 AW3423DW. By definition, it hasn't been possible to test recently released panel generations over several years. But each new generation has arrived with promises of improved burn-in resistance.

If that's an overview of generic OLED tech, what about the specifics of the stuff available to buy? It turns out all OLED gaming monitors use panels from just two sources, LG and Samsung. Strictly, there is a new player just arriving on the scene, TCL CSOT, and with it a novel so-called inkjet OLED tech. But there's little to nothing you can actually buy right now with that technology in the gaming space.

So, LG and Samsung it is. LG's tech has broadly been branded "WOLED", where the "W" stands for "white", while Samsung's panels have been branded "QD-OLED", with the "QD" referring to quantum dot technology. Whether you buy an OLED monitor from Asus, MSI, Alienware or anywhere else, it'll use one of those two basic panel types.

Indeed, until recently, it's been relatively simple to generalise about the two options. LG's WOLED panels used an additional white subpixel to boost peak brightness. Samsung's QD-OLED, meanwhile, had the edge for colour volume and vibrancy, thanks to its strategy of sticking with standard red, green and blue subpixels. Quantum dot tech also more efficiently converts the blue light generated by Samsung's emissive OLED layers into coloured light, compared to the simple filters LG uses to convert white light into coloured light.

Both shared essentially the same near-instantaneous 0.03ms pixel response. Combine that with high refresh rates and the result is razor-sharp motion clarity. However, there were and remain some further detailed differences. Samsung QD-OLED suffered from so-called purple tinting in bright ambient light due to the structure of the panel and the use of quantum dots, which can be activated by ambient light. Basically, stick one of the first three generations of QD-OLED panel next to a window on a bright day and it turns a bit purpley-grey, compromising black levels and overall contrast. On the other hand, the colours in LG's WOLEDs could look a little washed out, due to the use of that white subpixel to boost brightness.

Over those early panel generations, LG also had the edge when it came to image sharpness. Computer OSes like Windows function under the assumption that the subpixels in a digital display are arranged in a vertical RGB-stripe arrangement. LG's "RGWB" stripe, or red, green, white and blue subpixels arranged in vertical stripes, was much closer to that ideal RGB-stripe than Samsung's QD-OLED panels, which had an oddly triangular RGB subpixel structure. The upshot was that those triangular subpixel QD-OLED panels suffered from text fringing and a very slight softness in image quality, comparatively.

However, much of that has changed for the most recent generations of panels released in the last six to 12 months. The hot new thing, at least in terms of branding, is "tandem" OLED technology. Thus, LG has its new "Tandem WOLED" panels and Samsung has "Penta Tandem QD-OLED" tech.

In both cases, you might imagine the "tandem" bit implies fully dual-layer OLED panels, like those used by Apple in its iPad Pro tablets and the new PROLED MacBook Pro display. But actually, it refers to added emissive layers within the subpixels. LG's latest panels actually now have four layers, while Samsung's have five, hence the latter's pointed "Penta" branding flex. Either way, the added layers are claimed to increase brightness and improve durability.

Early monitor models based on either OLED panel type (like the aforementioned OG Alienware) tended to top out at around 250 nits of full-screen brightness, which I'd argue wasn't really good enough. The newer "tandem" generations have upped that to 300 and 335 nits for Samsung and LG respectively, which is closing in on the 400 nits I personally think is required to consider the full-screen brightness problem solved. Just note those figures are for pure white brightness, a metric that naturally favours LG's panels with their added white subpixel.

When it comes to colour brightness - and, in practice, most images you look at in-game are coloured, not pure white - Samsung's QD-OLED tech is often brighter. Don't, then, assume a higher outright brightness rating means brighter games. It's more complicated than that. The arrival of the Samsung Penta Tandem QD-OLED generation also brought with it an improvement, but not a total eradication, of the purple-tint issue in bright ambient light.

If you've followed all that. and honestly, props if you have, I'm afraid to say this is where things get really baffling. Both LG and Samsung have also released pure RGB-stripe subpixel variants of their newest "tandem" OLED panel tech. For LG, that means dropping the white subpixel for the sake of both better colour volume and more precise rendering, but slightly to the detriment of peak brightness. For Samsung, that means a switch from the triangular subpixel arrangement to vertical RGB-stripe and mostly just an improvement in pixel precision and text quality.

Not all of these panel types are available in all shapes, sizes and resolutions. But it gets confusing really fast. Right now, for instance, there are no fewer than six different 32-inch 4K OLED panel types to choose from. From LG you can have its original RGWB WOLED in, say, the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCDP, the new RGWB Tandem WOLED (for instance, the Asus ROG Strix XG32UQWMS) and then finally the RGB-stripe variation on Tandem WOLED ( see the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCWM). From Samsung, meanwhile, you can choose between its original triangular subpixel QD-OLED (like on the MSI MAG 321UP), the Penta Tandem follow up (of the MSI MPG 321UP X24) and then the all-singing RGB-stripe Penta Tandem (of the MSI MPG OLED 322URDX36, which is just about to be released).

Just to complicate things even further, LG's RGB-stripe "tandem" panels are still branded "WOLED", because the "W" in WOLED doesn't and has never referred to the white subpixels LG had hitherto used, but instead the white colour of the light produced by the emissive layers within each subpixel before conversion by the RGB filters. Got that? Phew.

The long and short of all this is that if you're comparing the very latest "tandem RGB-stripe" panels from LG and Samsung, they are closer now in terms of the subjective experience than ever before. Up until this generation, I always favoured QD-OLED for its superior colour vibrancy while accepting the purple tint issue. But as I peck out these words on the new 39-inch 5K2K Alienware AW3926QW and its Tandem WOLED RGB-stripe panel, I think I might just lean LG right now for its superior contrast in bright ambient light conditions, as well as this slightly more neutral subjective colour balance.

Anyway, as much as all that may feel like an exhaustive (and exhausting) dissertation, there is actually a fair bit I don't have space to fully cover. There are slight variations in the panel types, for instance, in terms of issues like uniformity and graininess, colour shift as opposed to outright burn-in, and also OLED flicker. But I wouldn't consider any of those even near to being deal breakers.

Really, it's just the long-term outlook that would have me thinking twice. First, that involves burn-in. I'd be pretty confident of getting at least three years out of an OLED. The big brands all have three year burn-in cover in any case (which is a very good reason to favour a big, familiar brand that you can be fairly certain will honour that warranty down the road). And it wouldn't surprise me if five years was very doable with the latest panels. The catch is that you can't, currently, be entirely sure about that.

Second, OLED technology is developing fast. It's come a long way in the last few years and I suspect that the next few will see comparable progress. Two or three years from now, I think full-screen brightness will likely be a totally solved problem, for instance, burn-in will be barely any concern at all, and prices will have come down even further. Ultimately, however, I wouldn't let that expectation stop me buying an OLED. It may not be entirely without flaws. But OLED is still by far the best PC display tech available today.

Peter Moore says this is "more than the release of a hugely anticipated game"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As GTA 6 brings in rave reviews and – predictably – takes over the internet as millions of players dive into Rockstar's long-awaited blockbuster, industry veteran Peter Moore says "the video game industry could really use a moment like this."

Moore, who previously served as president of Sega of America, corporate vice president of Microsoft's home and entertainment division responsible for Xbox marketing and operations, and CEO of EA, has taken to Twitter in the wake of Rockstar's latest launch. First, he offers an AI-modified image of himself with a GTA 6 tattoo in place of his infamous GTA 4 tattoo, which was revealed at E3 2006 to confirm the game's simultaneous launch on Xbox 360 and PS3.

But "in all seriousness," he adds, GTA 6's launch is an important one, and not just for the fans who've been waiting 13 years to play a new Grand Theft Auto game.

"We've been through a challenging period," he acknowledges. "Studio closures, redundancies, canceled projects and enormous uncertainty have taken their toll on an industry that has given so much to so many, myself included.

"That's why the launch of GTA VI feels so significant," he continues. "It's more than the release of a hugely anticipated game. It's an opportunity to remind the world of the extraordinary power of this industry to create, innovate, entertain and bring people together."

As someone who's spent so much time in the games industry, Moore says, "I've seen this industry reinvent itself time and time again." With that in mind, he hopes GTA 6 is able to deliver "the commercial success we all expect, but perhaps more importantly, I hope it provides a much-needed shot in the arm (no pun intended…) for the entire ecosystem: developers, publishers, studios, retailers, technology partners and the next generation of creative talent." After all, he says, "The games industry has always been at its best when it dares to dream big."

Well, as far as things go on the commercial front, it looks like the game has had an extremely strong start. Rockstar hasn't revealed any official figures, but with analysts' old launch week predictions going as high as $5.2 billion, and more recent estimates placing the revenue as of yesterday at $1.65 billion, it's safe that plenty of folks are buying it.

#3783. PlayStation defeats £2 billion UK lawsuit that alleged Sony forced consumers into "excessive and unfair prices"

12.2 million gamers can be wrong, apparently.

Sony has defeated a major £2 billion UK class action lawsuit concerning the price of games on the PlayStation Store (thanks, TheGameBusiness). The judgment came after a 30-day Competition Appeal Tribunal that took place in London, where PlayStation users claimed Sony had removed "all actual and potential competition" in relation to selling digital games on the console.

The case, brought by Alex Neill, who said she represented roughly 12.2 million gamers, accused Sony of applying "excessive and unfair" pricing on games that appeared on the storefront accessible by PS3, PS4 and PS5 consoles - the PlayStation Store. In a judgment published by the London’s Competition Appeal Tribunal today (17th November), the case was rejected. The judgement noted that market definitions used to define Sony's conduct were "unsafe", and that consumers "would be likely to make informed choices when purchasing consoles" and games on the hardware, too.

"Potential PlayStation console purchasers had both access to sufficient information and an incentive to consider that information in order to make informed purchasing decisions at the console level, especially in the case of high-value users who spend significant amounts in the digital gaming aftermarket," read the judgment.

The lawsuit made the argument that, upon purchasing a PS5 or other PlayStation console, you were then trapped within its ecosystem, and forced into paying the prices determined by Sony. The Tribunal disagreed, however, and ruled that Sony competed within a wider 'systems market' alongside Xbox, Nintendo and PC, for example. Furthermore, the Tribunal found no evidence that the existence of other digital storefronts would have actually brought any PlayStation Store pricing down.

Interestingly, the Tribunal used the argument that consumers can also opt and buy physical games instead of using the PlayStation Store - something that is changing as of the start of 2028. That did not seem to have any bearing on today's decision, though. It's also worth noting that this case did not seek to interrogate the ownership status of digital games - something that's been at the heart of the movement rallying against Sony's decision to kill off physical media. Earlier this year, spokespeople from Sony's legal team argued "reasonable consumers" already know they don't actually own their digital games.

The London Tribunal has a fairly long history. Back in 2022, it began as a case that attempted to sue Sony to the tune of £5bn for "ripping people off" on PlayStation Store. Sony argued the case brought against it in this trial was "flawed from start to finish". This isn't the only situation where we're seeing consumers pursue legal action against the platform holder. Last year, PlayStation was sued in the Netherlands over the so-called "Sony tax" that highlighted artificially inflated prices on the Store, and sought to represent more than 20,000 participants that felt short-changed by the company.
