#3649. Timothée Chalamet Talks ‘Dune 3,’ the Knicks, and His Hollywood Inspirations

Shoes on or off?” Timothée Chalamet asks, like any good New Yorker entering someone’s apartment. On is just fine.

He’s carrying a white paper deli bag—“starving,” he says—so I set him up at the dining table, where he unfurls a Lenwich Italiano. He devours it in less than two minutes. We’ve met before, but definitely never hung out at home. I think he’s friends with Frank Ocean, so I throw on Channel Orange. I had stocked up on a variety of beer and tea, can offer a coffee or a cocktail, but Chalamet wants New York City tap water, please, no ice.

Custom jacket by Haider Ackermann for Canada Goose; pants by Roa Hiking; backpack by Montbell.

I live in a one-bedroom in the East 60s, the second floor of an 1870 town house. The walls are white, the floors are black, and there are flowers from the bodega on the coffee table.

Chalamet is in earth-toned gorpcore, from the sand-colored Gnuhr puffer all the way down to a tawny pair of Roas, and would look equally at home camouflaged on the streets of Manhattan or trekking in the Dolomites, which he has recently done with his father. Both ears are pierced. Except for a navy blue novelty tourist cap which reads, in a comically fancy font, “Hvar, Croatia”—another recent vacation destination, with girlfriend Kylie Jenner—Chalamet’s color palette is pure Arrakis.

THE PROPHECY Timothée Chalamet, who will reprise his role as Paul Atreides – the chosen one – in Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three, photographed in Iceland. Shirt by Prada.

He’s just come from the Fiorello H. LaGuardia High School of Music & Art and Performing Arts, his alma mater located directly across the park, where he spoke with a group of drama students. Tonight he’s going to a Yankees game with his mom, the former New York City Ballet prima ballerina, and his sister, Pauline.

Late lunch concluded, he relocates to the sofa. “Ahhh,” he says, taking a big seat and resting his right arm along the back.

He glances down at the old issues of Vanity Fair on my coffee table and comes to a stop on one in particular: June 1995. Courtney Love is on the cover, photographed by Herb Ritts, wearing massive white-feathered wings in homage to the Nike of Samothrace at the Louvre. Inside, there’s a Ritts portrait of a toddler Frances Bean.

OUTDOOR VOICE Timothée Chalamet and photographer Aidan Zamiri spent three days in Iceland for this shoot, code-named Caladan—the planet where Chalamet’s Dune character, Paul Atreides, was born.

“This wasn’t the crazy one,” I say, guessing at what he’s thinking.

Three years prior to this cover, in the September 1992 issue of Vanity Fair, Lynn Hirschberg profiled Love and quoted her saying that she used heroin before and at the beginning of her pregnancy. The story sparked a crisis for the young Cobain family that resulted in an investigation by the department of children and family services and Cobain threatening Hirschberg and her dog. In the annals of celebrity profiles, it goes down as one of the most scalding of all time.

Chalamet knows all about that story because he’s seen Montage of Heck, the Cobain documentary that features the Vanity Fair article. “It was mind-blowing to me because Lynn has only ever been to me just a figure of warmth...” Chalamet says, trailing off.

He puts the magazine back slowly, like it might burn him.

I’ll be honest with you: That’s not what’s about to happen here today. I’m not that scary, and he’s not using heroin. Nevertheless, this guy’s jumpy.

It’s dangerous business for a movie star to open his mouth these days. Chalamet knows that better than anyone. At 30, he’s been famous his entire adult life. He’s dating one of the most visible women in the world. And he is acutely aware how a single comment in Vanity Fair could ricochet around the pinball machine of the internet. Earlier this year, during a no-holds-barred Oscar campaign for Marty Supreme, an offhand remark comparing the film industry to ballet and opera was met with outsize outrage, as some saw an opportunity to take Hollywood’s boy wonder down a peg. Those aware that he’s from a performing arts family knew what he meant. (“Is he wrong?” New York Times’ dance critic, Gia Kourlas, asked.) He doesn’t want to revisit that with me, perhaps because as he enters another awards season, he’s cautious in a way that only comes with experience.

In our 90 minutes together, Chalamet is both earnest and also reluctant to be profiled. He is by turns generous and guarded, confident and careful. He prefaces answers to no fewer than seven different questions by saying that he doesn’t want to sound “pretentious.” Truthfully, he never does. He’s protective of his personal life and will not discuss his girlfriend, nor much outside of filmmaking. “I wish I didn’t have to talk too much,” Chalamet says. And yet here he is, all across Iceland in our cover shoot, and now on my blue velvet sofa.

Like every conversation in late 2026, ours starts with AI. “Thou shall not make a machine in the likeness of a man’s mind,” Chalamet reminds me, is one of the opening lines of Dune, Frank Herbert’s seminal 1965 sci-fi novel. The story takes place in a world where computers are banned long after an AI apocalypse like the ones that are presaged by current-day tech CEOs and causing so much societal agita.

COLD MOUNTAIN Chalamet formed a community while making the first two Dune films. The third was “a more claustrophobic, isolated experience.” Boots by Timberland; scarf by Norlha; vintage pants by Arc’teryx Pro.

Chalamet tells me he’s reading The AGI Chronicles, tech journalist Kevin Roose’s new book that maps out the sprint to reach artificial general intelligence. He points out that the first four chapters of the book track the plot of Artificial, referring to Luca Guadagnino’s new Sam Altman biopic. “This is five seconds ago.” He recommended the book to Marty Supreme director Josh Safdie, who later tells me Chalamet “found it to be not only informative, it’s helped with anxiety. The more you know, the less anxious you are about it.”

Just when everyone seems at least a little bit anxious about the end of the human species, along comes Dune’s computer-free vision of the future that is, as Chalamet puts it, “strangely superhuman, strangely very human.”

LIFE ON MARS “The whole thing is daunting,” says Chalamet about working on a franchise like Dune. Coat and shoes by Prada; pants by Stone Island.

You don’t need to have seen the conclusion of Denis Villeneuve’s trilogy to understand a few things about it. First of all, that it is enormous. Its scale is even bigger than The Odyssey’s. The grand vision of Villeneuve’s intergalactic war drama actually makes the adaptation of the West’s first epic poem (and presumed best picture front-runner so far) look like an exercise in restraint.

The production design of Dune: Part Three, set 20,000 years in the future, is largely inspired by the pangeographical past. There are aesthetic references as far-ranging as the samurai and SEAL Team 6, the Roman Empire by way of the Third Reich, Islamic extremism and the Russian Orthodox Church, the Bedouins and the Asaro mud men of Papua New Guinea, and perhaps more than any other single culture, ancient Egypt. And like the pyramids themselves, the visual effect of the film is mystical rather than technological, even though both obviously are technical achievements. (No AI was used in the making of Dune: Part Three.)

Chalamet gives Villeneuve all the credit for what he calls the “titanic” scope of the film, constructed on the foundation of the first two over the course of a decade. “It seems like he just kept building and becoming more ferociously in control of it,” he says. “Much like how Paul gets good at riding the sandworm, Denis took hold of these films.” The movie makes it easy to see how Star Wars—and particularly Anakin Skywalker’s character arc—is often considered derivative of Dune. (For the real heads: The story of Dune: Part Three is roughly equivalent to Star Wars episodes IV through VI, all in one film.)

“It’s huge, huge geography,” Chalamet says. “Do you think you could have done this when you were in your 30s?” Chalamet asked Villeneuve on set. “He goes, ‘No way.’ ” The director went on to tell him that he passed on a “huge sci-fi project” earlier in life that he wouldn’t even reveal to Chalamet, but Villeneuve “turned it down precisely because he felt like he didn’t have the tools yet.”

Production designer Patrice Vermette’s life-size sets were so imposing that Chalamet spent time on location in Budapest ahead of the film’s shoot, immersing himself in the palace of Arrakis so that he wouldn’t be distracted by its grandeur when the cameras rolled. “The whole thing is daunting,” Chalamet says. “I didn’t want any part of the day to be lost to ‘Wow, look at what I’m stepping into,’ ” he adds later. Compared to shooting the first two Dune films, he was more or less alone on set. Chalamet remembers it as “a more claustrophobic, isolated experience.” The way Villeneuve puts it: “Timothée created a bubble around himself which allowed him to delve more deeply into the depressive darkness of his character.” He was, after all, preparing to play a murderer.

FIELD OF VISION According to Chalamet, Dune, which is set 20,000 years in a computer-free future, feels “strangely superhuman, strangely very human.” Hoodie and eye cover by Adon; T-shirt by James Perse Los Angeles; necklace by Blackmerle.

Part Three encounters Chalamet’s antihero, Duke Paul Atreides (also known by his Fremen alias Usul, as the religious cult figure Muad’Dib, and the Padishah Emperor of the known universe—you got all that?), at the height of his totalitarianism and the nadir of his soul. Sixty-one billion is the number of deaths attributable to Atreides, who in the Herbert novels compares himself to Adolf Hitler and Genghis Khan. He is a “psychopath,” according to Florence Pugh’s Princess Irulan. Villeneuve tells me there was another detached paranoid figure he compared Atreides to: Howard Hughes.

To get into character, Chalamet studied the personalities of world leaders—“everyone good and bad” and particularly “megalomaniacs across human history.” He notes that “Frank Herbert wrote Messiah to course correct...the first Dune, where Paul is sort of revered as a hero.” He continues: “This is a cautionary tale against cults of personality and figures of charisma.” When I ask if Donald Trump was on his mind, he says “not particularly,” noting that power and its corrosive effects on the soul are “eternally prescient themes.” The film is ultimately a story of atonement—if not redemption—for a fallen messiah.

It was all this research that compelled Chalamet to shave off his globally recognized curly mop. “Decision fatigue is a real thing amongst the world leaders, good and bad, current and past.... The idea of not having to change clothes, not having to sweep the hair out of your face, simple shit like that.” And so Chalamet said goodbye to his Samson-like locks. Did he feel...“like Anne Hathaway in Les Mis?” Exactly. Or Natalie Portman in V for Vendetta, I offer. (He loves V for Vendetta.) Perhaps Demi Moore in G.I. Jane. “We would [shave] it basically every other day. My hair grows quickly, so we would get after it.” Today the curls, as you can see, have returned to their natural state. Power restored.

“Timothée has become much more ambitious as an actor,” Villeneuve tells me when I ask how he’s changed in the decade that they’ve worked together. “He is exploring new artistic paths in a highly exciting way.” Costar Javier Bardem says, “In a way, his growth has been almost chronological with that of his character. In Dune: Part Three, there is a real gravitas to him. He stands firmly in his place, with a confidence and authority that he has earned through his work, his sacrifices, his dedication, and his commitment as an actor and as a professional. You can see it and feel it, and it is incredibly reaffirming to witness.”

Safdie puts it like this: “I believe he’s like hi-fi sound. A good hi-fi system you can listen to in a tiny room and it makes the room feel huge. And he has that ability as an actor...his style of acting is larger-than-life realism.”

“He is always restlessly searching to keep the scene alive,” says Greta Gerwig, who directed Chalamet in Lady Bird and Little Women.“He needs room to scream a scene or whisper it or jump up onto a table or pirouette.”

MAN OF ACTION Chalamet wants his art to speak for itself: “My work is my bones and muscles. I have little interest in putting more of myself out there.” Suit by Gucci; shirt by Harvey Bigg.

When I ask Chalamet if being famous his entire adult life prepared him to play a lonely-at-the-top emperor, he points to the moment in the first Dune when Paul and his mother, Lady Jessica, arrive on Arrakis and are greeted by the entire awe-inspiring army. “There were moments” in his own life, he says, when he realized about his relationship with the public: “Oh, something has shifted.”

Wandering around my apartment, Chalamet is observant and interested. “The picture in your bathroom looks like Greta.” He means Gerwig, though it’s actually Edie Sedgwick balancing on one leg in arabesque, cigarette in hand. (Sedgwick lived in this apartment during her Warhol years, and the picture was taken in the living room where we are sitting.) We look through the 1965 issue of Vogue, in which the picture originally ran.

He points out the French poster for The Graduate in the bedroom, in which a pink Matisse-like cutout of a woman’s elegant leg hovers in a thought bubble above Dustin Hoffman’s head. “I didn’t know it was called that,” he says. “Le Lauréat.” (One journalist recommended that I speak French with Chalamet, as they find him more open when they do. Sadly, I can hardly order dinner in French.)

He loves an Annie Leibovitz picture of Cindy Sherman made up as the sad clown in Edward Hopper’s 1914 Soir Bleu and points out monographs about Ed Ruscha and Harmony Korine on my bookshelf. (“Beast!” he declares about Korine.)

He sweetly asks me about a picture of me officiating my best friends’ wedding.

WORLD VIEWS “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland, you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central,” says Chalamet, a born and raised New Yorker.

We’re back on the sofa now. I’d asked Chalamet to do a little homework before our meeting: to come prepared to talk about his favorite movie performances. He was a diligent student, but instead came with four films and one play that specifically helped him get ready for his Vanity Fair cover shoot.

“Tree of Life,” he begins, citing Terrence Malick’s impressionistic masterpiece as the “biggest inspiration” for the cover shoot, photographed by Aidan Zamiri over three days in Iceland. “It could have been accomplished over a half day in the studio,” Chalamet says, but they traveled thousands of miles because, as in Tree of Life, “the process is almost as important as the finished product.”

Next up is One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest. “It’s a kick-ass performance, and it’s provocative and heartwarming and full of life and one of the great movie performances of all time.” He cites Cloud Atlas, which the Wachowski sisters made years after The Matrix trilogy, as achieving the kind of scale that inspired the team to trek to the edge of Icelandic cliffs and inside waterfalls. (It’s also one of two films, along with Bruce Robinson’s 1987 Withnail and I, that Christopher Nolan has ever recommended to him.)

Chalamet whips out his orange iPhone—where he has incidentally started a new daily habit of playing chess—to show me the trailer for the Francis Ford Coppola–produced 1982 art house film Koyaanisqatsi, a hypnotic succession of increasingly uneasy urban vignettes, sped up and slowed down. “It’s about the humility you must feel as any person within the scale of the universe,” Chalamet says. “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland, you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central.” This one was recommended by Safdie and is clearly an inspiration for the relentless, kinetic pacing of his own movies as well. Chalamet is so close to Safdie that even the chess habit is inspired by the match that Safdie and Alfonso Cuarón continue in perpetuity.

“What’s interesting about Timmy is he’s incredibly curious and very sincere, but also has a pretty sharp sense of humor and can be quite jagged,” Safdie himself tells me a week later. “There’s a goofy seriousness to him. He likes to be provoked.”

SMOKE SHOW Next up for Chalamet? A top-secret collaboration with a “phenomenal” filmmaker. “It’s kind of a no-brainer.”

And finally, he gives me Man to Man, Tilda Swinton’s one-woman show currently on at London’s Royal Court Theatre. “It’s about the incredible futility of existence and a person losing their mind,” Chalamet says. “I liked it in this little program I created.”

I’ve never met any actor who prepared for a photo shoot the way he would for a role in a movie. I get the sense that’s just Chalamet’s way: Everything he does in public is considered part of the art. Everything except, perhaps, courtside appearances.

Little provokes Chalamet more than the New York Knicks, and it is the subject about which he gets most animated. “It’s the most quintessential New York team” for many reasons, he says, but chief among them is location, location, location. “It’s not like the Yankees or Mets, Giants, or Jets. It’s in the heart of Manhattan, and it reflected the agony of the New York experience for decades.” Chalamet says he lives two lives: one as himself and one as “fan with a capital F.”

When I ask what his greatest extravagance is, the immediate and definite answer is “sports tickets.” “Those away games weren’t cheap, but...it is the most fun I’ve had in my life as a human.” We know this. Because the best word to describe pictures of Chalamet courtside and in the Knicks locker room is simply ecstatic.

He tells me about traveling through the night from San Antonio back to New York after the Game 5 championship as an all-time life high. “I flew with people that had been working at the Garden for decades,” he says, explaining that Ben Stiller and Fat Joe were along for the ride on an MSG-owned plane. (“I don’t want to sound too out of touch,” he worries. I assure him the reader will understand that commercial airlines aren’t running 2 a.m. departures.) “It was just incredibly raucous, everyone celebrating.”

DISTRESSED OUT Or is he? Chalamet isn’t pressed about trying to emulate his heroes: “It’s less sexy to some degree to wade out in the unknown, but it’s more authentic.”

Chalamet says he will always remember Jalen Brunson’s quiet leadership as the hallmark of the season overall. “It was not the cult of personality” you might expect to lead a championship team, he notes. “It was someone actually quite soft-spoken, reserved, and hardworking, and unassuming.”

On topics other than basketball, he is less enthusiastic. “My work is my bones and muscles. I have little interest in putting more of myself out there,” he says. What’s something that no one asks you that you wish they would? “Nothing. I mean, nothing. I’m not being passive-aggressive about this interview at all, but I think...” he trails off. Chalamet points at the speaker, which is still playing Frank Ocean. “He’s one of the rare people where the vacuum of what’s out there about him helps drive the...” “Curiosity?” I offer. “Beyond curiosity, how brilliant his artistry is. But the economy of movies,” Chalamet says, thinking. “You got to sell a lot of tickets.”

Which is exactly the reason that we’re sitting here together now. Who is his dream collaborator, living or dead? After a long silence, I tell him he can pass. “Okay. Pass.” What does he think of David Ellison’s Skydance taking over Warner Bros., the studio behind Dune? “I’m going to hit a Frank Ocean and be mysterious,” is all he says.

Leonardo DiCaprio once gave him very solid advice. Two rules: no superhero movies, no hard drugs. Would Chalamet have any advice for a 22-year-old getting started? “I think the best thing you can do is encourage people to be confident in what they believe is best for them.” Plus, he adds, “the Kane Parsons of it all brought me tremendous humility,” referencing the 21-year-old YouTuber turned director of the staggeringly successful Backrooms.

He’s vague about future projects. “I got one thing with a phenomenal filmmaker,” he says. “It’s kind of a no-brainer project, and should it get announced, I think you’ll see what I mean.”

Would he ever return to the character of Elio, the protagonist of Call Me by Your Name that gave him his star turn? “A great question. Never say never, but...I’ve grown up with the mindset that you don’t really go near something that is so near and dear to people.” So, that’s a no. “Now, to work with Luca again? In a heartbeat.”

GAME BOY As Chalamet sees it, there are two ways of living his life: one as himself and one as “fan with a capital F.” Jacket by Chrome Hearts; headlamp by Nitecore.

Is there any actor, or artist of any kind, after whose career he would like to model his own? “Who was [Bob] Dylan looking at? Dylan.” He broke the mold, I offer. “He created the mold.” Chalamet wants to be an original too (and perhaps this is what he meant when he declared that he was in “pursuit of greatness” at the 2025 SAG Awards). “It’s less sexy to some degree to wade out in the unknown, but it’s more authentic,” he says. “Especially in the movie industry where people could feel like, Oh, that was the golden age.... You gotta cook it up in a unique way.”

Around 6 p.m., Chalamet gets up off the couch and suits back up in his gorpcore. The Yankees game starts in just a couple of hours, and he has to shower and collect his mom and sister and make his way to the Bronx. I walk him downstairs, amble down the stoop, and almost want to say: Look! We survived!

#3648. Cara Delevingne Is 'Lucky' to Have Girlfriend Minke After Recent Surgery

Cara Delevingne opened up about her recent health struggles, revealing her partner, Minke, has been a godsend through it all.

Delevingne, 34, exclusively told Us on Wednesday, November 18, that Minke (real name Leah Mason), 27, has been her “biggest support system in this era of life,” explaining, “She sees me in and through everything.”

“I think I’ve never been able to be the most me until I’ve been with her,” the model shared while attending the L’Oréal Paris Women of Worth Celebration.

Delevingne called the musician her “biggest supporter, my biggest champion” and someone who has had to put up with a lot.

“Oh, I feel so bad for her sometimes, man, I don’t know. I really do feel so bad for her,” Delevingne said, noting that she had undergone an endometriosis procedure 10 days prior and Minke “had to look after me.”

Endometriosis is an “often-painful condition in which tissue that is similar to the inner lining of the uterus grows outside the uterus” and often affects the ovaries, fallopian tubes and the tissue lining the pelvis, according to Mayo Clinic.

Delevingne noted that the condition “sucks,” but she is feeling “OK” following the surgery.

“Being a woman is hard sometimes, man. But we’re here. We keep fighting,” she told Us. “We keep going, and we love it. Listen, I love being a woman. It’s incredible.”

While Delevingne is currently on the mend, she confessed that after the procedure, her “hormones have been everywhere,” and it was Minke who was able to comfort her.

“I’ve been working so much. I wasn’t recovering properly, well, because I had been working so much,” she recalled. “And she’s there, and she’s by my side, and she loves me, and I love her.”

Delevingne noted that Minke’s continued care and kindness during her health ups and downs has only strengthened their relationship.

“I can’t wait to have a family with her. I’m just, I’m very lucky that she’s in my life,” she gushed.

Delevingne and Minke have known each other since they were kids at boarding school. The pair reconnected more than a decade later at an Alanis Morissette concert and went public with their romance in 2022.

“Two magical years with you and so many pictures of us kissing in front of things ❤️,” Delevingne wrote via Instagram in June 2024. “These past two years have been A LOT of life. A lot of change, growth, pain and most importantly LOVE and I am so lucky to have found the perfect person to ride life’s ups and downs with.”

While Delevingne has found The One in Minke, she told Us on Wednesday that she has also learned to take L’Oréal Paris’ “You’re worth it” slogan to heart.

The company has been recognizing extraordinary women leading nonprofit organizations and “creating meaningful change” in their communities at its annual L’Oréal Paris Women of Worth for 21 years. This year’s honorees each received a $25,000 grant in partnership with Points of Light.

Delevingne said that believing in her own abilities and knowing your worth doesn’t have to be a big to-do.

“It’s got to come from within. If you’re not able to evoke that feeling, rely on your friendships. Remind yourself. Get into your body,” she said of her tips to feeling confident. “I always think if I don’t feel worth it, I’m in my head. So I’ve got to get out of my head and into my body.”

Delevingne pointed to dancing or “anything that makes you laugh” or cry or get angry as keys to getting out of your head.

“Something needs to move, and I think, yeah, self-worth comes through that. You know, it doesn’t always have to be pretty,” she added. “It needs to be real and ugly, and whatever it needs to be, it should.”

#3647. Penn State Alum Indicted for Allegedly Distributing Cocaine to Fraternities

A former Penn State student was indicted by a federal grand jury on narcotics distribution charges after he was accused of being “major supplier” of cocaine to the school’s fraternities in a drug trafficking ring scandal.

United States Attorney Brian D. Miller and Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday announced in a Wednesday, November 18, press release that Agostino Abbatiello was charged with one count of conspiracy to distribute cocaine and six counts of distribution of cocaine.

The federal prosecutors said that Abbatiello, 24, was the largest dealer of cocaine on the Penn State campus and that he was responsible for distribution of more than 11 pounds of the drug from January 2023 through December 2024, which went to the Sigma Chi and Delta Upsilon fraternities.

Abbatiello was allegedly both a dealer and frequent user of the cocaine, and he’s been accused of continuing his operation even after law enforcement launched an investigation into drug trafficking on the campus.

He allegedly purchased cocaine from suppliers in Philadelphia and New York and recruited others on campus to help him obtain the supply and transport it to the college.

Once he got the cocaine to the campus, Abbatiello allegedly had other fraternity brothers and pledges prepare and package it for resale.

“College should be a marketplace of ideas and not illegal drugs,” Miller said in a statement. “Our office will continue working with the Pennsylvania Attorney General’s office, and with our law enforcement partners to identify, investigate, and hold accountable those who profit from illegal drug activity in our communities.”

Sunday added that the “defendant was the top rung of the ladder for a high-level drug trafficking ring that supplied cocaine to Penn State University students, incorporating some fraternity pledges into the packaging process.”

“We are proud of the fine investigative work involved in building this case, thank the grand jurors for their diligence, and look forward to having a hand in prosecuting with our ready and able partners at the U.S. Attorney’s Office,” Sunday said.

Abbatiello has pleaded not guilty to the recent indictment.

The Westbury, New York, native previously pleaded not guilty in August when he was hit with 11 state charges in Pennsylvania, including corrupt organizations, conspiracy, dealing in proceeds of unlawful activity and manufacturing or delivering drugs.

Abbatiello was one of 14 people who has been charged in state court in connection to the drug trafficking ring at the college.

His lawyer, Philip Masorti, did not immediately respond to Us’ request for comment.

#3646. GTA 6 Has A Surprising Late Game Cameo That Knocked Me On My Ass

Across social media and YouTube, a massive spoiler from the final chapter of Grand Theft Auto 6 has been spreading online. It is a cameo by a past character that has people going wild. Some fans who have sped through the game’s story are rushing to be the first to share it online. Others don’t believe it’s even real. I’m here to confirm that, yes, the wild cameo you saw is real, and it made me scream.

This is your last warning. The next paragraphs are going to completely reveal the spoiler. If you are a massive GTA nerd and/or love surprises, stop reading now and close this article. Seriously, you’ll thank me later. For those who don’t care about spoilers, GTA lore, or who were never planning to play the game, let’s dive into one of the biggest surprises hidden within the massive world of GTA 6. Last chance to turn away. See you on the other side.

Near the tail end of GTA 6‘s big, epic crime story, Jason and Lucia begin working with Giorgio, a wealthy shipping magnate. He’s been working with some cartels and Eastern European criminals and has been letting them use his ships to smuggle cocaine across the ocean. It’s been working out pretty well for a while, but by the time Jason and Lucia show up, the Coast Guard has seized all the drugs from a recent shipment. He has a plan to rob the Coast Guard, get his coke back, and make everyone happy before they come to his big penthouse and kill him. But then, just as his big heist is coming together, a higher-up from the Balkan criminal family he’s been working with shows up to put a bullet in his brain.

And the person sent to Vice City is none other than Grand Theft Auto IV protagonist Niko Bellic. Yup. As shared online by many players already, a much older Niko shows up in two cutscenes to threaten Giorgio and then to collect the drugs once the heist works out. Here are those cutscenes:

I will admit that before he showed up, when I heard Giorgio yell out, “Daddy’s back bitches!” I chuckled to myself and thought, “Oh nice, a reference to the opening line of GTA IV. Cute.” I had no idea that would be followed up by the reveal of fucking Niko Bellic. I might have let out a scream and paused the game in pure shock and amazement.

We’ve not heard much about Niko since the ending of GTA IV. So seeing him back in the flesh, with grey hair, was great. And I love that Rockstar got back the original voice actor, Michael Hollick. And yes, that’s why in the credits of GTA 6 posted online by Rockstar, he is simply labeled “The Hitman.”

I can’t wait for more GTA fans and nerds to discover this moment and share their reactions. I’ll have more to share about the cameo and how it came about soon from my interview with Rockstar Games head of production Rob Nelson. But for now, let’s just enjoy the fact that Niko is back, baby.

There are few movie franchises as popular as the Marvel Cinematic Universe, which is constantly expanding thanks to new projects arriving in theaters and streaming with a Disney+ subscription. While there's always excitement about upcoming Marvel movies, the Avengers: Doomsday is on another level entirely. The public recently got another look at the Doomsday cast via new posters, and fans aren't holding back their thoughts about one hero's appearance.

What we know about Avengers: Doomsday is limited, which is why fans are devouring every photo, clip, and tidbit of information as they come out. We recently got our best look yet at Alan Cumming's return as Nightcrawler, reprising his role for the first time since 2003's X-2. Check it out below:

First look at Nightcrawler in ‘AVENGERS: DOOMSDAY’. https://t.co/78RMOU1SgJNovember 18, 2026

Alan Cumming might be clueless about Doomsday, but he's finally entered the chat with the above poster. This is the clearest look we've gotten of the X-Man's design, apart from a brief glance in the Avengers: Doomsday trailer. It's quite different from his look in the second X-Men movie.

Unfortunately, fans who spent years watching the Marvel movies in order haven't exactly been kind about the Emmy winner's appearance in the image. They made their voices known in the comments section of the above post, with some responses reading:

Ouch. There are also plenty of memes in the responses as well, including the of-used clip of Steve Buscemi saying "How do you do, fellow kids?" from 30 Rock. Some fans aren't responding to Alan Cumming's new look as Nightcrawler, including his mane of white hair. And yes, there are plenty of folks comparing his appearance to late actor Gene Wilder.

The makeup itself is quite different from X-2, and reminds me of how Mystique's look was similarly changed for Jennifer Lawrence in Dark Phoenix. It's a lighter blue, and is presumably much easier to apply. Alan Cumming was previously quoted talking about the change in makeup, saying:

I’ve had some makeup tests already for the role, but what’s great about it was that before, it was about four and a half hours to apply it, but now it’s only 90 minutes.

That's a huge difference. Of course, the hours that it took for X-2 really paid off, as Alan Cumming (and Rebecca Romijn) looked incredible in that sequel. We'll just have to wait and see if fans change their mind when they get to see Nightcrawler in all his glory.

All will be revealed when Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters on December 18th as part of the 2026 movie release list. I'm still hyped about seeing the forthcoming crossover movie, even if some fans aren't happy about Nightcrawler's look.

#3644. Timothée Chalamet Came Over for Lunch—and a Cover Story

The history of actors appearing in Vanity Fair goes back about as far as the movies themselves. Making a studio-orchestrated, Edward Steichen–captured debut in the pages of this magazine was a milestone in the careers of Gary Cooper, Gloria Swanson, Anna May Wong, and dozens of others, many of whom never made it to Technicolor.

On more than one occasion, the idea of Timothée Chalamet as the last male movie star has been a debate here at the office, usually ending in uneasy agreement: He is one of very few left, maybe the only one of his generation. He is in the tradition of Marlon Brando and Leonardo DiCaprio in that his knowability runs inverse to his fame. Like other endangered species, his extreme rarity makes him celebrated and isolated in equal measure. And with each of these stars, one rule usually holds true: The bigger they get, the less they open their mouth.

All of which is why we are thrilled to have Chalamet on our cover as he sets out to open the final, breathtaking installment of Denis Villeneuve’s Dune trilogy. He and our team, led by photographer Aidan Zamiri, fashion editor Taylor McNeill (with whom I was an assistant at this magazine in 2010), and VF global creative director Jennifer Pastore, trekked to Iceland for a multiday shoot to capture his cover story “A Star on Planet Earth.” Everyone involved—including and especially Timothée—approached it more like a film, or maybe a music video, than a typical cover, and there is a spiritual quality that runs throughout the pictures. “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland,” Timothée tells me, “you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central.”

Timothée also had the idea that I write the cover story myself, and while I was reluctant, I eventually thought, Why not mix it up? He came over to my apartment in early October for a conversation about Dune; his career; the careers of other actors, musicians, and painters; and especially the careers of the New York Knicks. I took away from our meeting that he may be a movie star, sure, but he approaches everything as an artist. The writing process is a humbling one, though—okay, it’s agony—and since filing the cover story, I have come to believe that every editor really should write a feature now and again to make us more understanding of our writers. Perhaps once a year. Consider it a new rule at Vanity Fair.

Timothée and I were both reading Kevin Roose’s The AGI Chronicles when we met up, and he pointed out that the first several chapters of the book might as well have been the source material for Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s new film starring Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov. The film presents a villain origin story of OpenAI’s cofounders, particularly CEO Sam Altman. It is the natural inheritor to David Fincher and Aaron ­Sorkin’s 2010 film, The Social Network, which similarly helped answer the how-did-we-get-here question for another quite recent era of technology.

In case you missed it, Altman was recently on the cover of Vanity Fair, sitting atop our revived New Establishment list. It inspired a torrent of furious reader feedback, including a few death threats. I understand that those messages were rooted in genuine fear of this technology and ire toward its Dr. Frankenstein founders (and me, by extension, for covering them). But reporting on the powerful—whether power is granted by elections or equities or zettaflops of compute—has always been the mandate of this magazine and will continue to be. We’ll keep the movie stars too.

#3643. Rockstar Founder Issues Rare Statement As GTA 6 Launches To Superb Reviews And Huge Sales

We might not hear from him much, but Rockstar co-founder Sam Houser remains highly involved with the studio and its games, and that includes GTA 6, which is available now in New Zealand and everywhere else on November 19.

To mark the game's launch, Houser released a statement in which he said Rockstar has once again tried to create a game in GTA 6 that "exceeds your expectations" and shows "what this medium is capable of, and why we believe games are so special."

He told GamesRadar: "Rockstar Games was founded on the belief that games could achieve the same distinction as all other forms of storytelling, become essential to modern culture, and to be thought of as stories and worlds that live on with us."

The executive went on to say that he hopes GTA 6 feels "both familiar and entirely new," and above all else, something that people find to be fun.

"This is a narrative set in a world of possibilities--and it is up to you as the player to shape how it ultimately feels, and concludes," he added.

Finally, Houser reminded people that GTA 6 might be the pinnacle of the franchise so far, but Rockstar isn't closing up shop anytime soon.

"We look forward to many more years of sharing these experiences with you," he said.

It's possible it won't be another 13 years for the next GTA game, as Rockstar's owner, Take-Two, has said the "nature and velocity" of GTA releases will change.

Sam Houser rarely releases statements, gives interviews, or appears in Rockstar's promotional efforts, so even this celebratory statement is notable. GQ writer Sam White recently posted a series of tweets (and then deleted them) saying an interview he had planned with Sam Houser fell apart at the last minute.

On GTA 6, Sam Houser was involved in every aspect of the game's creative process.

Sam Houser's brother, Dan Houser, left Rockstar in 2020 after the successful launch of Red Dead Redemption II. He started a new company, Absurd Ventures, which is working on an open-world comedy game that will be revealed soon.

GTA 6 arrives for everyone on November 19, and it's expected to be a massive success, the likes of which the industry hasn't seen since ... 2013's GTA 5. In GameSpot's GTA 6 review, Tamoor Hussain said there might not be another game like it until the inevitable GTA 7.

#3642. Country Singers Ella Langley and Tucker Wetmore's Relationship Timeline

Ella Langley and Tucker Wetmore have spent most of their rumored romance dodging direct questions so far, letting side-by-side vacations, tour bus cameos and flirty Instagram comments do the talking instead.

Us confirmed in September 2026 that the Nashville-based country singers had been “quietly dating for more than six months but less than a year,” though further details remain unknown.

Scroll below for Langley and Wetmore’s low-key relationship timeline:

Langley and Wetmore were first linked after being spotted vacationing together in the British Virgin Islands. The sighting kicked off dating rumors that neither artist immediately publicly addressed.

Dating speculation gained steam when a TikTok user posted footage of Langley boarding Wetmore’s tour bus after the two performed together at a charity event in Chattanooga, Tennessee. The clip surfaced just days after Wetmore appeared on Kristin Cavallari‘s “Let’s Be Honest” podcast and claimed he had “sworn off blondes.”

Later in the month, the pair traded flirty comments on Instagram. Langley wrote, “Cute fish” beneath a shirtless photo of Wetmore fishing in Australia, and he replied, “This is good” on a video of her performing an acoustic version of “Loving Life Again.”

A source confirmed to Us that Langley and Wetmore had been “quietly dating for more than six months but less than a year,” explaining that the two met organically in Nashville.

“They run in the same circles, so they met naturally through mutual connections,” the insider said. “It started casually, so they kept it on the DL at first, but they’re more serious now. They’ve met some of each other’s family and friends. It’s going really well.”

The source added that Langley “has been grateful for Tucker’s support and guidance” as she navigated a career-defining year.

Later that month, the couple were photographed leaving the 2026 Nashville Songwriter Awards together, hours after Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” logged its historic 23rd week at the top of the Hot 100.

Before the month came to an end, Langley brushed off a viral date request from influencer @TikiBeen1, who asked, “Ella, how many likes to take you on a date?”

“Not enough in the world,” she shot back, without mentioning that she was off the market.

Wetmore has stayed similarly tight-lipped. When a concertgoer asked about the relationship during a Q&A session, he responded, “Next question.”

Langley and Wetmore walked the red carpet separately at the 60th annual CMA Awards at Bridgestone Arena in Nashville. Langley wore a beaded, plunging Elie Saab dress, while Wetmore opted for a striped, double-breasted Amiri suit paired with a black cowboy hat.

Langley arrived as the night’s most-nominated artist with nine nods, while Wetmore was up for New Artist of the Year. While neither star publicly confirmed their relationship on the red carpet, audiences got a glimpse of Langley rocking out in the crowd to her man’s live performance.

#3641. How Long Does It Take To Fly Across The Entire GTA 6 Map?

The Grand Theft Auto 6 map is absolutely massive, gigantic, and at least one more synonym to encapsulate its size accurately. Whether it's land, sea, or air, covering it is going to take a lot of time, but just how many hours should you set aside for a flight across Leonida?

We found out for ourselves by piloting a single-propeller plane across the map, which took us an entire four minutes and 10 seconds between the two points on the map. That's pretty big!

We've known for a while that the GTA 6 map was going to be big--with roughly more playable space than GTA 4, GTA 5, and Red Dead Redemption 2 combined--but even that claim doesn't put into perspective just how enormous the game truly is until you experience it for yourself. Another fascinating tidbit is that escaping GTA 6 is nigh-impossible, but definitely worth attempting.

As one streamer has discovered, if you try to cheese it on water using a jet ski, you'll run out of fuel and be left stranded in the water. There might be a happy ending to this scenario, as some streamers have posted clips of a dog on a wave runner coming to their rescue. We've tried to replicate this ourselves, but we've had no luck yet.

But if you choose to stay within Leonida's invisible boundaries, you won't run out of things to do for quite some time. Between missions to improve your lot in life, pursue relationship goals, and soak up the scenery, the reactive open world of GTA 6 will keep you entertained for hours. Our GTA 6 review gave the game a rare 10/10 score, and dozens of other reviewers worldwide have also been very impressed with what Rockstar Games has achieved.

You can experience all of that for yourself soon, and if you're not planning to do some digital tourism with a long walk, check out our GTA 6 guides hub for all kinds of walkthroughs to help you survive and thrive in the game.

The Terminator is getting older, but apparently nobody told Santa.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I've accepted that Arnold Schwarzenegger can probably do things at 79 that would put me in physical therapy. Still, watching him take time from his busy 2026 movie schedule to hoist an enormous Christmas tree overhead while dressed as Santa Claus made me do a double take. The moment comes from a new Santa Schwarzenegger holiday ad, which follows the action icon through New York City in a Santa suit as he dodges the paparazzi. Somehow, he winds up helping a family load a tree onto their car. I suspect some movie magic made that lift possible, but seeing Arnold casually handle an entire evergreen is pretty funny. It also has me wondering: What's it like doing stunts at his age?

The Santa clip landed on Arnold's Instagram just days after the former governor got candid about what action scenes feel like at his age. During his November 11 appearance on Jimmy Kimmel Live!, Schwarzenegger discussed the possibility of returning to Predator, Commando, and Conan the Barbarian. Kimmel brought up King Conan, which would follow his famous warrior as an older ruler whose reign is threatened. When the conversation turned to the demands of filming that kind of movie, Arnold admitted the years have made a difference:

I tell you one thing, to do all this action and the sword fighting and horseback riding, and all this stuff is not as easy anymore today than it was 40 years ago…. Well, you get older and you slow down a little bit, right?

Four decades ago, Schwarzenegger swung swords and ran through jungles. I'd imagine climbing onto a horse in full costume feels a little different at 79. Of course, he wasn't about to let a serious observation about aging ruin a perfectly good joke. He quickly followed up with a line that had me laughing:

No, not very much. But still, I'm now at an age where it takes me an hour and a half to watch 60 Minutes. Unbelievable, I think. Things are really slowing down.

That's a pretty fantastic old-man joke. The timing is even better when you remember this is the same guy currently showing up in Amazon’s holiday commercial looking capable of bench-pressing a Christmas tree. Kimmel also commented on how muscular Schwarzenegger still is, which led to some playful back-and-forth between the two. Even the Terminator is still perfectly comfortable being the butt of his own jokes.

A post shared by Arnold Schwarzenegger (@schwarzenegger)

Schwarzenegger isn't pretending he can simply pick up where he left off in 1986, either. He's spoken about how a potential King Conan would acknowledge the character's age, with Conan having spent decades on the throne before facing a threat to his kingdom. That's an idea I can get behind. CinemaBlend has already covered his updates about possible Predator and Commando sequels, although he told Kimmel he was still waiting to see finalized scripts.

Meanwhile, the Christmas tree is a nice bit of promotion for The Man with the Bag, Schwarzenegger's new Prime Video holiday movie with Reacher star Alan Ritchson and Awkwafina. In it, he plays Santa, who recruits a thief to recover his stolen bag of presents. The film arrives December 2 for anyone with a Prime Video subscription, marking his return to Christmas comedy 30 years after Jingle All the Way.

As for that tree lift, I'd love to see some behind-the-scenes footage before giving Arnold full credit for the feat. But the man seems to be having a blast playing Santa, and I hope he keeps finding excuses to do action scenes. Maybe someone can make him a really comfortable saddle for King Conan.

Ryan graduated from Missouri State University with a BA in English/Creative Writing. An expert in all things horror, Ryan enjoys covering a wide variety of topics. He's also a lifelong comic book fan and an avid watcher of Game of Thrones and House of the Dragon.

#3639. Jason Loves Cats In GTA 6, But Not All Of Them

Grand Theft Auto 6 co-protagonist Jason is, like many Americans, a fan of cats. Naturally, being an open-world game with seemingly endless possibilities, GTA 6 does indeed let Jason express that love by petting cats he sees. However, not every cat is down to be pals with Jason.

As shared on social media, if you're walking around Leonida and spot a friendly-looking cat, you can go give it a pet. Jason even talks to the cat, because you'd have to be a monster not to, and the action even gives him a little focus boost.

But not all cats are the same. Another clip shared online shows Jason carjacking someone, as one does in GTA. After driving away, loud meowing can be heard, and the camera cuts to inside the car as a cat viciously attacks Jason. A quicktime event is necessary to get the cat to stop, at which point Jason is able to stop the car and let the cat out.

We can only imagine what would happen if that were a Rottweiler in the back seat of that car and not a sort-of-large cat. There are plenty of other animals to kill you while you're roaming Vice City and the rest of Leonida in Grand Theft Auto 6, and most of those would be less embarrassing to mention in your obituary than "cat."

Grand Theft Auto 6 is one of the most expansive and detailed games ever made, and if you're looking for some help, you can check out our GTA 6 guides hub as well as our guide on what to do first.

In GameSpot's GTA 6 review, Tamoor Hussain said, "This game is the culmination of everything the developer has previously achieved in the open-world space that pushes the genre to heights that, in all likelihood, no other developer will be able to reach. GTA 6 is an astonishing open-world action game that I'd wager won't be outdone until Grand Theft Auto 7," ultimately awarding it a 10/10 score.

#3638. Who Killed Fashion Founders Bryan Walker and Michelle Min?

Panoramic Hill looms above the UC Berkeley campus, a tree-covered neighborhood cut by steep paths and outdoor staircases. Century-old homes by brand-name architects like Bernard Maybeck and Walter Steilberg dot the incline, which straddles the border of Berkeley and Oakland. Each residence is worth millions; increase the amount for the occasional bit of newer construction. Unlike the busy urban streets below, the area is incredibly quiet. That’s one of the reasons everyone heard the shots.

“I have that stored in my memory, as I will for the rest of my life,” Daniella Salzman tells me, looking out her window at the former home of Michelle Min and her husband, Bryan Walker. The couple, creators of the Bryn Walker clothing brand, were found just outside their residence around 10:45 a.m. on October 2, 2026, shortly after neighbors called 911 to report the sound of gunfire. Initial confusion about jurisdiction sent police from both Berkeley’s and Oakland’s departments to the scene.

By the time paramedics arrived, Walker and Min were dead from what OPD assistant chief Casey Johnson characterized as “apparent gunshots” in a press conference later that day. A firearm, he said, was located at the scene. He declined to offer further details on the case, saying that the department’s homicide division would handle the investigation.

Nearly seven weeks later, we still know next to nothing about how Walker and Min died. While OPD turned down my request to speak with Johnson, it sent me a press release with the same details he laid out on October 2. Follow-up questions were met with: “There are no updates being released other than the information below.”

Bryn Walker store on Vine Street in Berkeley, California.

“I don’t know what has publicly been shared or what privately has been learned about what took place,” Salzman says carefully. Police have been silent since the brief press conference the day the bodies were discovered. But Michelle Min’s brother, Paul Min, hasn’t been quiet.

Within two days after his 63-year-old sister was found dead, Paul spoke with outlets including the LA Times and the California Post, accusing his brother-in-law of killing his wife, then himself, following a series of disastrous financial decisions that led to significant losses and a collapse in his mental state. The interviews, given so soon after the crime, suggest Paul was still in a state of shock over his loss. Walker, who was 61 when he died, was “the most honest, responsible, hardworking guy you have ever known,” Paul told the LA Times. “I loved him like a brother.” Michelle “was utterly devoted to Bryan to the very end,” Paul told the Post, “and he shot her.”

After those interviews, which were published that first weekend in October, Paul fell silent too; I made multiple efforts to arrange an interview but was ultimately unsuccessful. But according to the Post’s interview, Walker “had quietly taken out loans against their properties, and had gambled on risky options and leveraged positions,” with estimated losses of “well over $100 million.” The debt, per the LA Times story, allegedly prompted Walker to suggest that he and the Min siblings “end things”—a proposal that alarmed the Mins, but only because of its implications for Walker’s mental health. Paul didn’t see Walker as a danger: “He said the idea that Walker would or could harm them was absurd to the two of them,” reported the Times.

The Mins came to the US from Korea in 1977, settling first near Kansas City. Michelle met Walker there in the 1980s, and after the Mins’ parents chose to move to California, the siblings, and Walker, followed. In 1992 the couple opened a clothing store in Berkeley that sold goods from other makers. As time went on, they began to manufacture more and more of their own goods.

Eventually, Bryn Walker evolved into a clothing brand known for loose linen looks with an Asian-meets-Swedish flair. “Flowy, a touch eclectic, made for perhaps older women who want to mesh elegant/sophisticated with a bit of boho uniqueness,” a longtime Berkeley resident told me over email. “Women who want to look expensive but with a bit of verve.” When I described the company to one San Francisco resident as “elevated Chico’s,” I got a stern look. “You better not let any of the Bryn Walker moms at Lowell hear you say that,” she said, referencing the city’s hotly competitive public high school. “These are not humorous people.”

Bryn Walker store on Fourth Street in Berkeley, California.

According to the Post piece, Walker “had stepped aside and allowed his designer wife to control their mutual business and his eponymous fashion label,” but it’s not clear when that management change occurred. As the brand grew, it struck a chord with fashion businesses across the country—from luxury boutiques to the family-run department store chain Dillard’s. Bryn Walker also opened its own brick-and-mortar storefronts beyond Berkeley.

Many of those stores are now gone. One Bryn Walker location in Santa Monica closed prior to mid-March of 2021, while a 22-year-old outpost in Palo Alto shuttered in 2020. On the East Coast, a shop in Edgartown, on Martha’s Vineyard, went dark in 2024. A call to its shop in Vineyard Haven was met with a recorded message saying the business would be closed until further notice. That leaves just two company-owned shops, both in Berkeley, where Bryn Walker began.

One of those stores is on Berkeley’s buzzy Fourth Street, a glossy shopping destination lined with outposts of national brands like Apple, Lululemon, and Herman Miller. With items generally priced between $130–$300, it fits right into the overall ethos of that street—and Berkeley—where almost everything is spendy but not flashy; theoretically accessible, though not to those on a budget. During my recent visit to the shop, the sole staffer remained pleasant even after I identified myself as a journalist—but her tone grew firm. “It’s all still too raw,” she said of the tragedy.

I asked if, as he’d said he would in his Post interview, Paul Min had taken over management of the company following its founders’ deaths. “I don’t know about that,” she replied, before declining to speak further. I was told by another local business owner that Bryn Walker employees are actively seeking other employment; it’s unclear what will happen to the label now that its creators are gone. I tried to reach Bryn Walker management by phone and email for this story, but did not receive a response.

Emilie Raguso was one of the first journalists to report on the deaths, for her independent outlet, The Berkeley Scanner. As she began investigating, she “saw that the number of open shops was different based on where you looked,” she says. “I was getting this early inkling of what others later reported as far as the business being in trouble.”

“The writing was on the wall,” she continues, “but there was nothing explicit. It did seem like, Oh, this is not a thriving business.”

Paul’s comments to the media didn’t address the health of the business. Instead, he was focused on Walker and Michelle’s personal finances, which he alleged were laid to waste by Walker’s mismanagement. “Your spouse lied to you and lost over $100 million and you might be out on the streets,” Paul told the Post. “You might go from being one of the wealthiest people in the country to being homeless because your husband lied to you and wagered everything on crazy bets.”

According to Paul, things grew so grim for Walker that the Mins spoke about institutionalizing him. But it’s also unclear how they would have acted on that without Walker’s cooperation. California enacted its CARE Court program in 2023, more easily allowing court-ordered treatment plans for those who might pose a threat to themselves or others. But in practice, courts have been reluctant to take that drastic step, frequently rejecting petitions from those closest to the person in crisis.

Bryn Walker-Pacific Cotton store on Main Street in Vineyard Haven, Massachusetts.

Speaking with the LA Times, Paul said that in Walker and Michelle’s home, he “found a note that lists a couple of [mental health] facilities. I speculate he saw that note or somehow figured out she was going to institutionalize him, but I have no idea.”

Paul’s claim that Walker killed Michelle over snowballing financial fears isn’t out of the realm of possibility, even in a place as wealthy as the Bay Area. One year before Walker and Michelle died, almost to the day, entrepreneur Paula Truong fatally shot her husband, Thomas, and their daughters, Mackenzie and Alexandra, before hanging herself in the garage of their $2.2 million San Francisco home. Reporting found that the family had experienced a string of financial challenges, including several failed business ventures, a home foreclosure, and a number of unpaid debts.

But that was in San Francisco—a sometimes gritty city that people escape with moves to places like Panoramic Hill. “When you get up into the hills, it does feel like a world apart,” Raguso says. “It feels insulated from a lot of the more common disturbances and things that we deal with down on the flatlands.”

Salzman has lived on that hill for more than 20 years, and she’s still struggling with the notion that her neighbor might have killed his wife. “Bryan was very engaged with neighbors who were needing support that were near him,” she says, characterizing him and Michelle as “committed to the community.” But she also believes that the fear of losing wealth can drive people to desperate acts. “We see wealth as being both our greatest need and our greatest opportunity here,” she says, “and we are told that we will be happy when we consume. This is the message that we’re given everywhere we look”—especially in a region with more billionaires than anywhere else in the world.

Raguso isn’t sure why Oakland police are taking so long to announce the results of their investigation. “At some point, there would be a ruling,” she says, citing possible delays with the medical examiner’s office as a reason things haven’t been resolved. According to Salzman, the vacuum of information has inspired her to look at all her neighbors with a little more care. “Part of what I awoke to was how little I know about really what’s going on with people that I’m geographically so close to,” she says.

“I just would have loved for there to have been a way to be a part of showing up for them, even around the little things. The more people that are aware of what is happening, the more people are potentially able to heal.”

#3637. Don’t Expect To See Vice City For A Long Time In GTA 6

For those still waiting for GTA 6 to unlock, it's possible you have something of a mistaken impression of what the early hours will look like. Despite partially sharing a setting with GTA Vice City, you should not expect to be walking up the game's equivalent of Ocean Drive and Miami Beach in the opening minutes, as in the 2002 game. Far from it.

As we noted in our video discussion on why we gave GTA 6 a 10/10 in our review, Tamoor and Jake did some expectation-setting. Rather than starting the game in Vice City, you'll instead spend the opening hours in a smaller corner of the state of Leonida, Key Lento. Vice City is undoubtedly the crown jewel of the game's world, but it could be as much as 20 hours before you reach it, depending on how you play.

This seems to be a deliberate decision that, as Tam says, allows you to progress through the world at roughly the same pace as the ambitions of co-stars Lucia and Jason. The opening area may not be as glamorous as Vice City, but it is no less detailed than the rest of the game. It's possible it's only meant to last you around 5-6 hours, but we found it easy to get lost spending far more time than that, which resulted in Tam not reaching Vice City until after 15 or 16 hours.

Key Lento provides a good look at how the game and its simulation work, letting you eventually progress to a much larger space (seriously, the map is huge) with a good understanding of how things work.

All of this is to say, the glitz and glamor of Vice City are waiting for you--eventually. To make the most of the opening hours, be sure to check out our guide on what to do in GTA 6 first.

#3636. Thomas Markle Competent to Stand Trial in Child Porn Case After Evaluation

Meghan Markle’s estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr., was found competent to stand trial amid his ongoing child pornography case.

Page Six reported on Thursday, November 19, that an independent competency evaluation by a psychiatrist determined that Thomas Sr., 82, has “sufficient ability to understand the nature and consequences of the charges against him” with a reasonable degree of medical certainty.

Federal Judge Lindsay Griffin reportedly said the update was being accepted into evidence, noting that it was uncontested. Thomas Sr.’s preliminary hearing in Florida is set for December 1.

Meghan and her father have been estranged since 2018, the same year she married Prince Harry. Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr., and Thomas Sr. relocated to Cebu Island in 2025 before moving to the U.S. earlier this year. Prior to returning in May, Thomas Sr. had his left leg amputated due to a blood clot. Thomas Jr. was reportedly his father’s primary caregiver since he suffered a stroke in 2022. Thomas Sr. is now reportedly living in a nursing home in Florida.

News broke in October that Thomas Jr. had found storage boxes containing suspected child sexual abuse material (CSAM) at Thomas Sr.’s home in the Philippines. At the time, Thomas Jr. told The Sun that he turned over the material to local authorities.

Thomas Sr. denied the allegations. He was arrested in Florida earlier this month on a federal charge of possession of child pornography. Thomas Sr. was released on bond the same day.

Investigators allegedly found material depicting child sexual abuse in two storage units registered to Thomas Sr. in Los Angeles, according to the Central District of California U.S. Attorney’s Office. The material reportedly contained photographs of a man believed to be Thomas Sr. with a young nude girl.

“The FBI and our partners have arrested Thomas Markle Sr. after an FBI investigation revealed he was in possession of Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM),” FBI Director Kash Patel shared in a statement.

Patel, 46, continued, “Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions. Working with our Justice Department partners, our agents moved quickly, identified and located the explicit material, and arrested Mr. Markle in Florida. This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids — any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide.”

Thomas Sr. was arrested earlier this month after he cut off his ankle monitor. He is also now facing charges in the Philippines with two counts of offering, distributing, selling, exporting or importing any form of child sexual abuse or exploitation material and one count of possessing such material, according to ITV.

Meghan shared in a statement last month that she learned about the allegations against Thomas Sr. in 2018.

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them,” Meghan said in a statement, in part. “I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.”

If you or someone you know is experiencing child abuse, call or text Child Help Hotline at 1-800-422-4453.

If you’ve been watching Jimmy Kimmel Live! – or if not live on social media – you should know commentary on President Trump and the White House in general has become an almost nightly occurrence. There’s a lot of history behind the contention, from Kimmel’s pointed jokes, to Trump and the White House’s bold insults, and FCC involvement in between. So, a Trump segment on late night? Not unexpected. Random shots thrown at the CMAs? A bit more surprising.

Last night Kimmel did spend a fair chunk of his monologue focusing on President Trump and Trump's recent visit to China. Though he made some comments about Communism, the weirdest thing he noticed about the visit was that the President seems to be wearing makeup on his hands these days to give him a little more youthful vigor.

This hand has been paved over more times than the Kennedy Center. Either that is makeup or he's eating peanut butter straight out of the jar again.

The Trump bit went on for a while in more traditional Jimmy Kimmel Live! style, and we'll have to wait and see if the President responds. Still, I was more amused this week by Kimmel trying to get in on the CMAs commentary. Let's get into the bobsledding joke, shall we?

OK, maybe I shouldn’t have been as surprised as I was to see Kimmel commenting on country music given the CMAs aired on ABC with a big, splashy Taylor Swift appearance (that led to some Swiftie theories). That's his own network, and it's nice to see him playing ball, even if some rumors have called his relationship with the network "unmanageable."

Sorry to everyone named Luke in Nashville, because Kimmel had all the jokes about some of last night’s major winners, including a sly reference to Luke Combs being in a long list of male country singers named Luke, also including The Voice's own Luke Bryan. (That whole convo gets weird too because while not named Luke, Zach Bryan is also a famous country singer. None of these people are related.)

The CMAs are the single biggest night of the year for guys named Luke. Number 1! Luke Combs scored three nominations, three more than his brother Sean Diddy, they had a tribute to Dolly Parton, of course. Brooks and Dunn got the Lifetime Achievement Award. It’s the highest honor in country music, named after the highest singer.

That last bit is a Willie Nelson joke, which is quite funny, but only if you already know the Lifetime Achievement Award is named for him. I did not see it coming though when Kimmel brought up bobsledding in regards to “Choosin' Texas.”

The big story this year is Ella Langley. She made history, her song “Choosin' Texas” spent 28 weeks at Number 1 on the Billboard charts, more than any song ever, and it’s still going. It’s still the No. 1 song. It’s been No. 1 since the Winter Olympics, which was mid February. This song has been No. 1 since the last time we thought about bobsledding!

Yeah, that’s a joke, but it’s also just the kind of absurd fact that’s worth remarking on. Ella Langley's crushing it, and this milestone is cool, but now I'll never think of it without also thinking of Olympics bobsledding. Sure, these are some fairly light jokes compared to his Trump stuff, but please don't say Mr. Kimmel never did anything for pop culture.

#3634. Bigfoot Is Back In GTA 6, And Apparently He Smells Revolting

Grand Theft Auto games have been home to some weird phenomena over the years, and in GTA 6, it looks like Bigfoot is back and stinkier than ever. As the game steadily rolls out worldwide--or as people digitally immigrate to New Zealand for early access--streamers have been posting clips online of their encounters with the cryptid, and this time, it doesn't look like a man in a suit.

It looks like the Bigfoot sighting is tied to a mission in GTA 6, as the mysterious creature is wandering the woods of Leonida and it takes off in a panic when you encounter it. Another clip shows a strange encounter in the woods, with the player interacting with an effigy that emits noxious fumes and knocks them out. In a brief cutscene, Bigfoots, uh, really big feet, can be seen approaching Jason as he drifts in and out of consciousness.

In that first clip, Bigfoot is also covered in a cloud of fumes, which likely references stories about the mythical creature's potent stench. For GTA--and Red Dead Redemption--fans, this isn't the first time that they've been involved in a Bigfoot sighting, as encounters with it stretch back decades.

Back in 2004, rumors began to circulate about Bigfoot existing in GTA: San Andreas, but Rockstar dismissed these reports as false in 2005. A few years later, in Red Dead Redemption's Undead Nightmare expansion, protagonist John Marston was tasked with hunting down a pack of Sasquatches, and it was eventually revealed that the creatures were peaceful, capable of human speech, and now going extinct thanks to a certain trigger-happy cowboy.

Bigfoot would appear in GTA 5, as getting 100% completion in the game would unlock a new mission where co-protagonist Franklin hunts down a creature in Blaine Woods, only to discover it was a man in a costume. As an extra joke, the Bigfoot impersonator drops a few references to Red Dead Redemption's infamous encounter, but that doesn't mean the real Bigfoot isn't lurking in GTA 5. You could use the thermal scope on the sniper rifle supplied to you to spot a bipedal creature watching you during the "Predator" mission, and eating a golden Peyote plant under specific environmental conditions would turn players into Bigfoot.

Red Dead Redemption 2 brought an air of mystery back to the Bigfoot mythos, as you could find a gigantic skeleton half-buried in the snow high up on Mount Shann, and protagonist Arthur Morgan could also speak to an unseen figure that was heavily implied to be Bigfoot.

Meanwhile, you can check out our GTA 6 guides hub for more details on how to make the most out of your trip to Vice City.
